Abbey is a vivid blue-violet that appears in Maerz and Paul's 1930 color dictionary, with no recorded reason for its name.
Acid green is a sharp, yellowish green whose history is thin, and the books read record the word more than the story.
Adelaide is a very dark violet from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary; the name is also a city and a woman's given name, and the books we hold do not say which, if either, it honors.
Adobe is the color of sun-dried clay brick, a muted reddish orange-brown; the name is probably borrowed from the brick itself.
Alabaster is the soft, fine-grained white stone used for vases, statues and painters' grounds, and the name of the warm cream that dictionaries have used for its look since the sixteenth century.
Algae is a clear, mid-light green named for the pond and sea plants it brings to mind, though most algae are not this color at all.
Alice Blue is a very pale, faintly cool blue-white, named for Alice Roosevelt and now one of the CSS and X11 color keywords.
Almond is a pale, warm beige-pink named for the nut and the tree, but the word has never meant one color: dictionaries use it for pink, yellowish brown and even grey-green.
Amazon is a deep forest green; in the jeweller's books the word names Amazon stone, a green feldspar.

Amber is the warm yellow-orange of fossil tree resin, named from the Arabic and, in Greek, the origin of the word electricity, and it has been traded across the Baltic for at least thirteen thousand years.
Amethyst is the violet-purple of a quartz crystal, a color word older than any pigment that tried to copy it, and one that painters seem never to have matched.
Amulet is a dark bluish green from the Maerz and Paul dictionary of color, named for the protective charm; the name's maker is undocumented, but the history of amulet colors is not.
Anemone is a muted rose-mauve named for the windflower, though the flowers themselves run from crimson to violet-blue.
Anthracene Green is a deep blue-green named for a coal-tar chemical, one of over a hundred color names that began on the chemist's bench.
Antimony yellow is a light orange-yellow named for a pigment made from antimony, usually the same lead antimonate that painters knew as Naples yellow.
Antique bronze is a dull, olive-leaning metallic brown meant to look like very old metal.
Antique Green is a dark, grey-green that mimics old objects, and a name that turns up on house-paint charts as well as in Ridgway's 1912 color plates.
Antique White is a pale, warm, yellowish white, now best known as one of the named colors of the web.
Antique is a dark brown-gold from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary; the word began as a trade modifier meaning made to look old.
Antwerp Blue is a nineteenth-century paint name for a pale, greenish form of Prussian blue, though earlier writers took it for a copper pigment, and it was never one fixed recipe.
Apple green is the fresh, yellow-leaning green of an unripe apple; it is one of the oldest object-names for a green, built into the mineralogists' color lists of the 1700s.

Apple is a bright, fresh green named for a fruit that most often is not that color; behind the name lies an older color word, apple green, which appears in natural-history charts as a pale gray-green.
Apricot is the soft orange-yellow of the fruit, a name that fashion and the pearl trade have used for a long time and that the old color books mention mostly in passing.
Aqua Blue is a vivid, bright cyan, a screen-era color named for the look of water.
Aqua green is a modern color name; Paterson defines it as a light bluish green, built on the web color aqua.
Aqua, as a color name on screens, means pure full-strength cyan, #00FFFF; it is the web name for a color that older sources call a light greenish blue.
Aquamarine is the pale blue-green of the gem beryl and the sea, and a web color whose screen version is far brighter than the stone.
Arcadian Green is a pale, soft green from the color card of the 1920s.
Armada is a very dark, warm brown, a textile color of the 1920s whose name recalls a fleet.
Arsenate is a deep blue-green that borrows the name of a chemical family, the salts of arsenic acid, whose members gave painters violets, blues, yellows and, by confusion, the famous poison greens.
Artichoke Green is a soft, greyed yellow-green, named for the vegetable.
Artificial vermilion is the same red mercury sulphide as natural cinnabar, made by combining mercury and sulphur, and for centuries it cost far less than the mineral.
Ash is the pale grey of what is left after burning, a color that old writers treated as colorless, that dyers and bleachers used as an alkali, and that painters borrowed as a name for weak pigments.
Asparagus green is a pale, greyed yellow-green from Werner's 1774 colour nomenclature for mineralogists, named for the vegetable but much quieter than a fresh spear.

Asparagus is a mid-light yellowish green named for the vegetable, and as a color word it is older than most people expect: it sits at number 58 in Werner's list of mineral colors as Syme published it in Britain.
Asphodel Green is a muted, yellowish green named for a flower of Greek legend.
Aster is a muted violet named for the star-shaped flower, recorded in Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary of color and dated there to 1916.
Atlantis is a dark, slightly greenish navy from Maerz and Paul's 1930 color dictionary; why it carries the lost island's name is undocumented.
Aubergine is the deep purple of the eggplant's skin, so dark on a screen that it reads almost black, and the name of a glaze on Ming-era Chinese porcelain.
Auburn is a reddish brown used above all for hair, and it began as a word for something paler: a yellowish or brownish white.
Auricula purple is a dark, reddish plum purple named for the garden auricula, and it entered the language of color when the painter Patrick Syme added it to Werner's chart of nature's colors.
Autumn is a dark, muted brown named for the season, recorded as a color in 1917, and a reminder that the fall palette is more varied than the one color name suggests.
Avellaneous is an old word for the light brown of a hazelnut, rare in speech but one of the commonest colors in the paintings of our archive.
Avocado Green is a bright, yellow-green, and a color-name whose meaning shifts with whose avocado you picture.
Avocado is the smoky yellow-green of the fruit's flesh, and for most people alive it means the kitchens and carpets of the 1970s.

Azure blue is a word that began as the name of a stone, the Persian for lapis lazuli, and ended as a name for the sky; the swatch on this page is neither, but a muted blue from Werner's 1821 color chart.
Azure is a bright, clear blue, the color of a cloudless sky, and its name is the Persian word for lapis lazuli passed through Arabic and Old French, long before it was a pigment or a flag.

Azurite is a bright blue copper carbonate mineral that painters ground into one of Europe's main blues before ultramarine and Prussian blue; the color name now points at a darker, duller swatch than the stone.
B'dazzled Blue is a Crayola crayon name, a pun on *bedazzled*, for a mid sapphire blue from the company's metallic line around 2000.
Baby Pink is a pale, soft pink, named for the nursery.
Bagdad is a very dark blue from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, using the older English spelling of the Iraqi city; why the city lent its name is undocumented.
Baltic is a very dark grey-green from a 1930 color dictionary, and its name carries no documented story.
Banana Yellow is the bright yellow of a banana skin, here as a vivid greenish yellow from the 2010 xkcd color survey.
Banana is a pale lemon yellow named for the fruit, and the books we hold say very little about it.
Barium yellow is the old pigment name for barium chromate, a light, greenish yellow that went by half a dozen trade names.
Baryta yellow is barium chromate, a dull greenish yellow pigment with a heap of trade names; the swatch in our library is a pale straw that stands for it.
Battleship Grey is a name for use, not for nature: the grey in which warships were painted, recorded as a color from 1912 and now a near-neutral mid grey on screens.
Beaver is a light, greyish reddish brown named for the animal's fur, a color tied to the fur trade, when Europeans coveted beaver pelts for their hat industry.
Beetle is a dark, greyed olive from a 1930 color dictionary, and the books have almost nothing to say about the name, but a great deal to say about beetles and color.
Beige Brown is a mid, warm brown with a hint of sand, a name used in several color standards.
Beige Grey is a mid-dark warm neutral, standardized as RAL 7006 in the 1927 color register and filed by ISCC-NBS as a grayish yellowish brown.

Beige is the French name of undyed wool cloth, borrowed in the nineteenth century for the pale yellow-grey of anything left in its natural state; once a color of poverty, it is now the color of the inoffensive.
Berlin blue is the German name of an early synthetic blue pigment, better known as Prussian blue, and in Werner's mineral colors it is the plate with the jay's wing and the blue sapphire.
Berry Pink is a deep pink-purple from Ridgway's 1912 plates, and its name has nothing to do with the old pigment called pink, which was yellow.
Berry Red is a deep purplish red; as a screen value it is identical to X11's maroon.
Berry is the name of a dark purplish red, but the word has lived many lives: it was a Greek name for an insect dye, and in the paint shop it meant a yellow-green buckthorn fruit.

Billiard is the deep green of the cloth on a billiard table, a color that arrived in the Maerz & Paul dictionary in 1930 and carries a surprisingly large share of the story of how people feel about green.
Biscuit is the pale tan of a baked biscuit, named from a word that means "twice cooked" and first used as a color in the 1880s.
Bismarck brown is a coal-tar dye from the aniline age, sold under several names and still used as a stain, which gave its name to a leathery brown.
Bisque is a pale pinkish or yellowish brown, a peach-tinted cream that became one of the standard named colors of web design.
Bistre is a transparent brown made from wood soot, used for pen-and-ink washes and for glazing shadows in oil.
Bistre is a warm, transparent dark brown made from the soot of burning beechwood, the wash that old-master draughtsmen reached for until sepia took its place.
Bittersweet is a hot coral-orange red, named for the plant whose berries ripen red and whose English name means a taste that is both sharp and sweet.
Black Blue is a near-black with a cold blue cast, a paint-card name whose root is the old trade term blue black: soot, charcoal and ink that lean blue.
Black brown is a brown so dark it is nearly black, a descriptive name that no color book treats as a color of its own.
Black Coral is a Crayola-list name for a dark bluish grey; the swatch looks nothing like black, and the books say little about the name itself.
Black Green is a very dark green-grey that looks nearly black, the name of one of the factory paint colours in the German RAL system.
Black Grey is RAL 7021, a very dark grey from the German paint-color system, so close to its neighbors Signal Black and Traffic Black that a screen cannot tell them apart.
Black Olive is a very dark, slightly green-grey neutral, the color of a ripe olive that has almost lost its green.
Black Red is a very dark red, so dark that it is close to black, listed as RAL 3007 in the German paint standard.
Black Shadows is a pale greyish pink in our data, which is a good reason to look at what painters learned about shadows: they are rarely black.

Black is the darkest color, the one a surface shows when it sends back almost no light: the color of soot, ink and night, which Europe has treated in turn as fertile, devilish, humble, luxurious, and not a color at all.
Blackish Brown is the last of the browns in Patrick Syme's Edinburgh color guide, a name inherited from German mineralogy and used by naturalists for feathers, nuts and pitch.
Blackish grey is a dark, almost neutral grey with a faint cool cast, a name from the colour tables that naturalists used before photographs, and the grey of a nuthatch's back.
Blanched Almond is a pale, warm cream, one of the named colors of the web.
Blood Orange is a deep, red-leaning orange named for the fruit with crimson flesh.

Blood red began as a plain description and was made a standard by eighteenth-century mineralogists, who listed it as a fixed color, and by Patrick Syme, who split it in 1814 into arterial and veinous blood.
Blue Bell is a pale, dusty violet-blue; its name could point to the flower, to a famous jeans maker or to a crayon, and no book we hold says which.
Blue Blue is a bright, slightly purplish blue that appears on Wikipedia's list of Crayola colors; its origin is otherwise undocumented, and no color book treats it as a named color.
Blue Grass is a very dark green in the Maerz and Paul color dictionary, and its name points at a plant it hardly resembles.
Blue green is the color halfway between the two, a deep greenish teal that English builds out of two words because it never had one of its own.
Blue-grey is a plain English compound for a grey with blue in it, and the swatch used for it here, a clear light blue, is only one of at least five competing versions.
Blue Jeans is a bright mid blue named for the washed look of indigo-dyed denim, a cloth whose fading made indigo a mass-market dye.
Blue Lilac is a muted violet that sits halfway between lilac and blue-violet, and Baty's color reference system pairs a similar shade with a flower, an insect and a stone.
Blue ochre is an old trade name, probably for the iron phosphate mineral vivianite, a rare blue earth that turns green with exposure.
Blue Turquoise is a light bluish green that the 1955 ISCC-NBS system traces to an older dictionary, and its archive matches are look-alikes rather than evidence of a pigment.
Blue-Violet Black is a very dark, nearly neutral grey with a faint cool cast, a shade of black rather than of blue.
Blue Violet is the bright web color named for the stretch of the spectrum between blue and violet, a place where painters, physicists and critics have all looked hard.
Blue is the color of a clear sky and deep water: a hue the ancient world barely named, the Middle Ages raised to heaven, and the modern West has picked as its favorite color for more than a century.
Blueberry is the color of the fruit, a deep violet-[[blue|blue]]; as a color word it is recent.
Bluish Black is one of the named blacks in Werner's nomenclature of colors, the system naturalists used to describe slugs, berries and ores before photography.
Bluish Green is a pale, greyed green that earns its place from an 1821 naturalists' chart, where it was swatch number 51, matched to a thrush's egg.
Bluish Grey is a grey with a cast of blue, a name that has been in colour vocabularies since the first mineralogists' charts of the 1700s and that, on screen, is barely blue at all.
Bluish Purple is a purple leaning toward blue, a name that began as entry 36 in Werner's nomenclature of colors and now marks a vivid screen violet.
Blush pink is a warm coral-leaning pink named for the color that rises in the cheeks when someone blushes.

Blush is the colour of flushed skin, and the word has two lives: in Paterson's dictionary it runs from red to a delicate pink, and in St Clair's glossary to a pinkish beige, while the swatch on this site is a much deeper pink.
Bole is a fine red-brown clay or ochre, best known as the smooth base laid under gold leaf, and a word that has meant several different earths.
Bone brown is a dull dark brown pigment made from partly burned bone, now obsolete, which also left its name on a modern greyish-brown.
Bone is a pale, warm off-white named for the bleached look of bone, and the same word names two old pigments, a gritty white and a brown-black, made by burning it.
Bordeaux is the deep, slightly bluish red of the red wines of Bordeaux, a port that was also a hub of the blue-dye trade.
Bottle green is the dark green of glass bottles, a name in use by the 1820s and later fixed on colour charts as a blue-leaning green.
Bramble is a dark, purple-tinged near-black named for the blackberry bush; the books know the plant far better than the color.
Bran is a warm tan, the brown of wheat bran, and a name the books mention more as a dye-vat ingredient than as a color.
Brazil red is an old name for a red pigment, listed in an eighteenth-century scheme of red colorants.

Bremen blue was a pale greenish-blue copper pigment of the nineteenth-century paint trade, so tangled with its cousin verditer that even specialists cannot say for sure where one ends and the other begins.
Brick Red is a color named for a building material, used by naturalists and dictionary-makers long before it became a paint-chart name, and its screen swatch is much pinker than any brick.
Brick is the dark orange-red of fired clay, a color so tied to its material that cities, dye shops and dress manuals all used the word long before anyone fixed a swatch to it.
Bright green is a description, not a historic name: on a screen it means the most intense green the display can show, and the swatch here sits almost exactly on pure screen green.
Bright Orange is a fully saturated, red-leaning orange (#FF5B00), a plain-language name that the books use as a description far more often than as a defined color.

Bright purple is a plain descriptive name for a vivid, saturated purple; it is a color of the synthetic age, because Ball reports that painters still had no pure, bright purple in the eighteenth century.
Bright red is the plain description for a luminous red, and the colors it describes, from cinnabar and cochineal to the postbox, tell how hard a lasting bright red was to make.
Bright Sky Blue is a vivid, slightly greenish cyan blue, a descriptive name more than a historical one.
Bright violet is a descriptive name for a vivid purple, and the best history the books offer is a very old theory of how violet is made.
Bright Yellow is a plain description, bright plus yellow, attached to a very pure, light yellow, and the phrase recurs in the books for gamboge, orpiment and the first coal-tar dyes.
Brittany is a mid steel-blue recorded by Maerz & Paul in 1926 and named, as far as the sources show, after the region of France.
Broccoli Brown is a dull, greyish olive-brown that earned its odd vegetable name in the colour lists of Scottish naturalists around 1800, long before it became a taupe on a paint chart.
Bronze green is a dark grey-green, and in old paint catalogs it was the trade name of cheap mixed greens rather than of one pigment.
Bronze is the brown of the metal alloy of copper and tin: darker and duller than gold, and the name of an age.
Brown Green is a very dark olive-grey, the name of a RAL factory paint colour, and in the books the same two words describe natural minerals, cotton and Chinese porcelain.
Brown grey is a descriptive name for a greyed brown, and its history is the history of dull cloth.
Brown Olive is a very dark, almost black olive-brown; as a name it echoes the old naturalists' olive brown, and as a color it is the dark ground of a great many paintings.
Brown Orange is a deep orange-brown, a descriptive name that shares its tone with iron oxide pigments and one rare brown-orange mineral.
Brown red is an old pigment name for the dull red made by burning yellow ochre, later borrowed as the name of a deep red-brown on color charts.
Brown Sugar is a warm reddish-orange brown named from a kitchen staple, one of hundreds of color names borrowed from food.
Brown is a darkened yellow or orange with a word of its own: the color of earth, wood and the poor man's coat, the oldest paint in the world and, for most of art history, the color of shadow.
Brownish grey is a plain descriptive name for a grey with some brown in it, and it has been used in color lists for two centuries.
Brownish Olive is a dull, dark olive that leans to brown, among the most common muted colors in old paintings.
Brownish Orange is a dark, red-leaning orange-brown, and the name is older than most of the paint that now wears it: it is entry 79 in a colour chart that Patrick Syme made for naturalists in 1821.
Brownish Purple Red is entry 97 among the reds in Werner's nomenclature of colours, a dusty rose-brown that the book matched to a bat's wing.

Brownish red is the plain description of a red darkened toward brown, and it is also a formal colour in Werner's mineral nomenclature, where it was number 99 and was matched to a bird's throat and a piece of flint.
Brownish yellow is the old descriptive term for a dull, deep yellow, the family of ochre and mustard, and in 1751 one fashionable shade of it was called caca dauphin.
Brownish is a hedge word turned into a color: a reddish mid-brown from Ridgway's 1912 color standards, named for a thing that is nearly, but not quite, brown.
Bruges is a dark, greyed blue named in the 1910s for the Flemish city, a town whose dyers, painters and jewelers each left a mark on the history of color.
Bruise is the color of a bruise: a dull, reddish purple that is named for the injury, not for any dye or pigment.

Brunswick green is a dark bluish green named for the German city of Braunschweig, where two brothers began selling a copper pigment in the 1760s; by the twentieth century the name meant a cheap mixed green, and then simply a color.
Bud green is a fresh leaf green named for the unfolding buds of spring.
Buff Orange is a soft yellow-orange from the colour lists of the early nineteenth-century naturalists, matched to a kingfisher's eye-streak and the stamens of a white cistus flower.
Buff is a light, warm yellow-tan named for buffalo leather, the soldier's coat color that George Washington carried into the American Revolution as half of buff and blue.
Burgundy is a dark purplish red named for the red wine of the Burgundy region of France, which also gave the name to a court whose fashion was black.
Burlywood is a pale tan from the X11 and CSS color lists, found in about one painting in twenty in our archive.
Burnt orange is a deep, reddish orange named in the spirit of burnt sienna and burnt umber, earth pigments darkened by fire.
Burnt Red is a deep, brownish red, named for the way heat turns earth pigments redder and darker.
Burnt umber is the reddish brown made by roasting umber, the manganese-rich earth whose name most likely means shadow; painters have used it for deep, translucent shadows since the 1500s.
Butterscotch is a warm golden orange named, it seems, for the candy; Paterson defines it as a yellowish brown and also indexes it among the yellows.
Byzantine is a vivid reddish purple named for the Eastern Roman empire, whose emperors guarded the real imperial purple: a dark, almost crimson dye that bears little resemblance to the bright swatch.

Byzantium is a deep reddish purple named for the eastern Roman capital, where the shellfish purple of Tyrian dye was a monopoly of the court; the screen color is modern, but the name carries the history of imperial purple.
Cacao brown is the reddish brown of the cacao bean, the seed behind cocoa and chocolate.
Cadet Blue is a muted greenish blue named for the grey-blue of cadet uniforms; it entered web color lists as one of the 140 X11 names.
Cadet Grey is a soft, bluish grey, listed by one dictionary as a variant name for cadet blue.
Cadmium green is the name of a composite artist's green, a blend of a cadmium yellow with viridian rather than a single mineral.
Cadmium Lemon is a bright greenish yellow sold in artists' tubes; it belongs to the cadmium family first made in 1820.
Cadmium Orange is a pigment made from cadmium sulphide, a rich, opaque and sun-proof orange of the nineteenth century, and the name that now also stands for a warm orange hue.
Cambridge blue is a pale, soft blue-green tied to the university and its boat-race colors.

Camel is a light, warm tan named for the hair of the camel, a color with a long history as the shade of poor cloth, and a name that books mention more for a wrong guess about a yellow pigment than for the brown itself.
Campanula Purple is a greyish blue-violet named for the bellflowers, one of the 110 colors in the nomenclature Abraham Werner built for minerals and Patrick Syme adapted for naturalists.
Campanula is the botanical name of the bellflowers, borrowed for a deep violet-blue; the books agree on the flower and disagree on whether the color leans blue or purple.
Canary is the bright, slightly greenish yellow of the songbird, a color that spent the nineteenth century moving from bird plumage to chrome-yellow paint on carriages and cabs.
Candida is a dusty rose-mauve, first recorded in 1925, with no documented link to its Latin namesake.
Candy Pink is a warm, strong pink listed in the 1955 ISCC-NBS system, and a name whose old and modern swatches differ a good deal.
Cannon is a very dark, slightly green-tinted grey, near gunmetal; its name is undocumented in the books.
Capri Blue is a deep greenish blue, named for the water of the island of Capri.
Caramel is a warm golden brown named for toasted sugar, and the same word also names a food coloring.
Carbuncle is the old name of the red gem that medieval writers said glowed in the dark, taken from the Latin for a small coal; as a color word it now labels a very dark reddish brown.
Carmine Red is the rosy red that Werner's color list gave as its characteristic red, named for the pigment carmine and handed down through Syme's English edition of 1821.
Carmine is a deep red with a slight blue cast, named for the lake made from scale insects, first kermes and then the Mexican cochineal; the same insect still colors lipstick, yogurt and Campari.
Carnation pink is a soft, light pink named for the carnation flower; the related word carnation had an older sense in painters' flesh tints.
Carnation is an old word for the color of flesh that settled on a warm pink, and it is also the name of the garden flower.
Carnelian is a red-to-orange variety of chalcedony, a quartz stone worn as jewelry and carved as a seal for thousands of years, and its screen swatch is a much deeper brick red than most carnelians.
Carrot red is a muted salmon-red; the name dates from the days when red carrots were grown.
Cathedral is a dark grayish purple from the Maerz and Paul color dictionary, a name whose origin the books do not record, set beside the real colors of medieval cathedral glass.
Cedar green is a sixteenth-century painter's name for a copper-mineral green, and today a dull, deep green on color charts.
Celadon green is a soft gray-green named, by the better-supported account, for a shepherd in a French novel of 1607, and later given to Chinese porcelain whose glaze takes its color from iron.
Celadon is a pale, grey-tinged green, named in seventeenth-century France for a shepherd in a novel and then attached to the grey-green glazed porcelain of China.
Celandine Green is a pale grey-green from Werner's system of colors for naturalists, where it stood at number 46 and was illustrated with a moth, a leaf and a gemstone.
Celeste is a very pale, cool cyan whose name means heavenly or sky blue; as a word it is older than the swatch, and the books that mention it use it for sky-blue pigments and cloth.
Celestial blue was a name in the paint shop before it was a color on a chart: a pale, reduced tint of Prussian blue, also used in French for cerulean.
Cellini is a deep red-violet in an old color chart, and our books do not explain the name.
Cement is a muted grey with a trace of green, the color of dried mortar; the books say more about the blue once sold for coloring cement than about the grey.
Cendre blue, from the French for ashes, is an old name for a pale copper-based blue, the pigment more often called blue verditer.
Cerise is the French word for cherry, borrowed into English as the name of a strong pinkish red.

Cerulean blue is the sky-blue paint of cobalt and tin oxides, a light greenish blue that reached artists in the 1860s and went onto the Impressionists' palettes. The swatch filed under its name here is a much deeper purplish blue, and that gap is part of the story.
Cerulean is a strong, slightly greenish sky blue, named for the Latin word for the heavens and made as a paint of cobalt and tin from about 1860.
Charcoal grey is the dark, slightly cool grey of burnt wood, and for a short stretch in the 1890s it was also a tube of artists' paint.
Charcoal is the dark grey of burnt wood, the oldest drawing black there is, from the bison of Altamira to the willow sticks in a modern art room.
Chartreuse is a bright yellow-green named for the liqueur made by Carthusian monks, and on the web it is the full-strength green at hex 7FFF00.
Chasseur is a dark forest green from the French word for hunter, recorded in the 1930 Maerz and Paul color dictionary.
Cherry red is the red of the fruit, a vivid, slightly bluish red that the word has named for centuries, though its oldest scientific meaning was darker and duller than the swatch.
Cherry is the red of the ripe fruit, a plain English name that mineralogists once used for a dark brownish red and that today means a bright, clear one.
Chessylite blue is an old name for azurite, the blue copper mineral, taken from the place in France where it was found.
Chestnut is the red-brown of the chestnut's shell, a word that also gave English maroon and still describes a horse's coat, a head of hair and a naturalist's chart color.
China Blue is two things with one name: an eighteenth-century English way of printing indigo straight onto cloth, and a dark blue in Werner's color nomenclature for naturalists.
Chinese red is an old trade name that has pointed at two different pigments: cinnabar from China, and a lead-chromate red made in Europe.
Chinese Yellow is a strong golden yellow, and an old trade name for the arsenic mineral orpiment, which China exported to the West.
Chocolate Brown is a dark, grayish reddish brown named for the food, and also the color that red lead pigment turns when it decays.

Chocolate Red is a dark brownish red, entry 98 in the color nomenclature that the Scottish artist Patrick Syme built from the mineralogist Werner's system, defined as a mixture of two neighboring reds.
Chocolate is the deep brown of the food made from cocoa, a colour name whose swatches range from a bright web orange-brown to something nearly black.
Chromium green is the name of green pigments made from chromium oxide, and old catalogs also use chromium-oxide names for viridian.
Cinereous is an old word for ashen grey, used above all of birds, and Ridgway's own swatch for it is a plain grey.
Cinnamon is the warm yellowish brown of the spice's bark, a color name that jewelers and pigment makers borrowed as well.
Citrine is a lemon-to-greenish yellow named for the citron, the color of the yellow quartz, and an old artists' word for a muddy tertiary between orange and green.
Claret is a deep reddish purple named after red Bordeaux wine.

Clay is the color of the material it is named for: a soft, slightly greyish orange-brown, closer to a fired flowerpot than to a river bank, because clay itself is a family of earths that can be white, grey, red or yellow.
Clematis is a bluish violet named for the flower, recorded in color dictionaries from 1899 on.
Cloudy blue is a descriptive color name, a soft grey-blue, and our books use it as a plain phrase rather than a named pigment.

Cobalt blue is the paint made by firing cobalt with alumina, worked out in Vienna, Freiberg and Paris between 1775 and 1802; the dark navy swatch shown here is a chart's sample of the name, much darker than a tube of the pigment.
Cobalt green is a pale, clear green made from cobalt and zinc, discovered in 1780 by Sven Rinmann and loved for its permanence but priced out of most painters' hands.

Cobalt is a deep, vivid blue named after a metal, and the metal after a mine goblin: the blue of Chartres glass and Chinese porcelain long before a French chemist made it into one of the steadiest paints ever made.
Cocoa is the brown of cocoa powder, a color name recorded by 1887, for a drink that began in the Americas and was once used as money.
Coeruleum is the older spelling of cerulean, the cobalt-tin blue that painters took up in the 1860s, though its story starts with an obscure German recipe from 1789.
Coffee is the dark, warm brown of the roasted bean, a color word taken from the drink; the books know it as a stain, a dye and a crop that took over from the dye plants.

Colonial is a dark, grayish navy that Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary filed under fashion and textiles; the books say nothing about the color itself, though a good deal about the blue dye trade its name recalls.
Commelina blue is a dye made from the dayflower, a small blue wildflower, and it was used in Japanese woodblock prints.
Commodore is a deep blue recorded in Maerz and Paul's 1930 color dictionary, with a name that is a naval rank.
Cool grey is a grey that leans toward blue, a distinction painters use constantly even though the swatch here is a pure neutral.
Copper Brown is a dark reddish brown, a name that in nineteenth-century pigment lists meant a brown made from copper compounds, not the color of the metal.
Copper red is a reddish orange named for an object, the kind of name early nineteenth-century naturalists used in their color lists and later dropped.

Copper is the reddish-brown orange of the metal, named after Cyprus; the strange thing is that the red metal has given painters almost nothing red, and instead most of the blues and greens of the ancient and medieval paintbox.
Coral red is a warm orange-red named for the skeleton of a reef animal, a hue the books treat mostly as a color word rather than a material.
Coral is the name of a sea animal's skeleton and of a warm orange-pink, once a red, borrowed from the precious coral that jewelers prized and that people wore as a charm.
Corinthian pink is a dusty, purplish pink that appears in color lists from 1912, long before it was a fashion word.
Cork is the light brown of the oak bark that stoppers bottles, and the same word once named a red-purple lichen dye and a bluish black.
Cornflower is the blue of the grain-field weed Centaurea cyanus, a bright blue with a little violet in it, and since the X11 color list it has been a stock screen color.
Cornsilk is a very pale warm cream, best known as one of the named colors of the web's X11 set.
Coronation is a very dark, reddish purple that appears in the 1930 Maerz and Paul color dictionary; the sources do not say who named it, but the ceremony it recalls has a long and mostly red history.
Cosmic latte is a warm off-white, the name two astronomers gave to the average color of the light of the universe.
Cosmos is a light reddish purple from the Maerz and Paul dictionary of 1930, named for the garden flower, and rare in painting.
Cotton candy is the pale sugar pink of the fairground sweet, and a crayon name that has become a color word.
Cranberry is a deep crimson-red named for the fruit.
Cream is the warm, yellowish off-white of the fat that rises on milk, a kitchen word that naturalists, quilters, paper-makers and tennis officials have all used for the white that is not quite white.
Creme is a very pale lemon yellow, brighter than the cream of everyday speech, and it keeps a French spelling for a color the English call cream.

Crimson is a deep red with a lean toward purple, named after the kermes insect whose dye made it one of the costliest cloth colors of medieval Europe, and later the color of cochineal, of cardinals and of the painter's transparent red glaze.
Crocus martis is an old name for an artificial iron oxide, made by burning iron, that painters and polishers used as a red or, in some recipes, a yellow.
Cyan blue was once a name for a cornflower dye recommended by Robert Boyle, not the printer's cyan of today.
Cyanine blue is an old name that meant a mixed pigment in the nineteenth century and, in Paterson's dictionary, a family of synthetic dyes.
Cyclamen is a bright pink named for the flowering plant; Paterson calls the flower's color red, pink or reddish-purple.
Dandelion is the vivid yellow of the flower's petals, named from the French for lion's tooth.
Dante is a near-black purple recorded in a 1930 color dictionary, with no documented origin for its name.
Dark blue green is a descriptive name for a deep, sea-dark teal, listed by the ISCC-NBS system in 1955.

Dark blue is the dark end of blue, and for much of history it was not a separate color at all: the word that gave us indigo and lilac first meant dark blue, and the Greeks counted blue as a kind of darkness.
Dark Brown is the deep brown of bistre ink, umber earth and old varnished shadow, a color that history kept mistaking for black, and that fills a quarter of the paintings in our archive.
Dark cyan is a web color: a deep blue-green defined in the X11 set and carried into CSS.
Dark goldenrod is an X11 web color: a deep, brownish gold that Paterson files among the browns.
Dark Green is the web color `#006400`, a deep, saturated green defined for the X11 and CSS color lists, and also the name of a whole family of darker greens.
Dark grey blue is a descriptive name for a deep, slate-leaning blue, and one dictionary uses the phrase to define Flemish blue.
Dark grey is the web-color swatch #A9A9A9, a name that adds dark to grey and, oddly, points at a light silvery grey that is paler than the middle of the scale.
Dark magenta is an X11 web color, a deep purple-pink that the ISCC-NBS system had already indexed in 1955.
Dark navy is a near-black blue, and one dictionary uses the phrase for a color it calls Nippon.
Dark Olive is a dim, grey-brown olive that sits between green and brown, and it is one of the most common dark colors in the paintings of our archive.
Dark Orange is a web color, `darkorange`, a saturated amber orange defined by the hex code FF8C00 in the X11 color set.
Dark Orchid is a vivid purple from the X11 color list, one of the standard named colors of the web.
Dark Plum is a very deep, reddish purple that is nearly black, named after the skin of the ripe fruit.
Dark Purple is the purple that nearly passes for black, the color Roman writers prized in the best shellfish dye and medieval dyers rebuilt with madder over blue.
Dark Salmon is a soft orange-pink from the X11 color list, built on the word salmon.
Dark Sea Green is a soft, grayed green, listed in the X11 set.
Dark Slate Grey is the web's `darkslategray`, a deep green-teal grey inherited from a 1980s Unix color list, and not, despite its name, a darker version of slate grey.
Dark Turquoise is a bright, saturated cyan-teal from the X11 color list, with little of the darkness its name suggests.
Dark Violet is a web color, `darkviolet`, a vivid purple defined by the hex code 9400D3 in the X11 color set.
Dawn is a pale, dusty pink named for the first light of day, a color word that has more history in poetry and in the sky than in any dye pot.
Deep blue is less a single color than a rank: the dark, saturated end of blue, a grade on the eighteenth-century dyers' scale and, since 1997, the name of a chess computer.
Deep Chestnut is a muted brick red, named for the chestnut.
Deep green is a plain descriptive name for a dark, saturated green, and the books mostly use the phrase to describe other, better documented colors.
Deep Malachite Green is a muted mid green with a name borrowed from the copper mineral, found in Ridgway's 1912 color atlas and in a modern table of nature's colors.
Deep Olive is a dark, yellow-brown green, a mixed color with a long record as a pigment and a dye; in our archive it is one of the commonest named colors on canvas.

Deep Orange-Coloured Brown is one of the descriptive color names used in the early nineteenth century to catalogue minerals, plants and animals, and it matches the red-brown of hematite and the cattail's spike.
Deep pink is a pink pushed toward red and magenta; as a screen color it is one of the loudest in the web palette, while in older books the phrase is a loose description for many rosy reds.
Deep red is a descriptive color name, a dark and saturated red; no book we read ties it to one pigment, dye or place, but its alternate names in old color lists are mostly iron-oxide earths.
Deep Reddish Brown is a dark chestnut with a trace of red, number 101 in the brown series of a nineteenth-century color chart for naturalists, and now also a plain descriptive name.
Deep reddish orange is the sixth and last of the oranges in Syme's 1821 edition of Werner's color nomenclature, a burnt, earthy orange defined by its goldfish, apple and topaz.
Deep Sky Blue is a vivid, light azure from the X11 color list, with sky blue as its parent entry in Paterson.
Del Monte is a muted grey-violet from the 1930 Maerz and Paul color dictionary, and the books say nothing about where the name came from.
Delft blue is named after the blue-and-white pottery of Delft in Holland, Europe's answer to Chinese porcelain; as a color name it has drifted from the pottery's bright cobalt to a soft, greyed blue.
Delphinium is a color named for the tall blue garden flower, a name that the chart-makers kept even after the swatch grew greyer than the petals.
Denim is the mid-blue of indigo-dyed cotton twill, the cloth of blue jeans; its name probably comes from a French town, though the books agree on little else about where the word began.
Desert Sand is a pale, warm, pinkish tan, the color of dry dunes in a crayon box and in the ISCC-NBS list; the books that mention desert sand more often call it red.
Dijon is a mustard-toned yellow-green named for a Burgundy city; the color books are silent on it, but the city shows up in them for a different reason, as the place where zinc white was worked out.
Dim Grey is a neutral mid-dark grey from the X11 color list, exactly 105 on each of red, green and blue.
Dodger Blue is a bright, saturated azure from the X11 color list, one of the web's standard blues.
Dove grey is the soft plumage color of the dove, and the books disagree on whether it leans blue, pink or purple.
Drab Grey is a light, warm, brownish grey from Ridgway's color atlases of 1886 and 1912, where *drab* means a dull, plain color with no brightness to it.
Duck green is the dark green of a mallard's neck and of yew leaves in the old naturalists' color charts, and also, confusingly, the name of a pale green in later dictionaries.
Dull Brown is a descriptive name, not a pigment or a place: a brown with the brightness taken out, which the color books mention only in passing.
Dull Green is a plain descriptive name for a mid green of low saturation, and as a painters' word it means a green with its chroma turned down.
Dull Lavender is a pale, greyed pinkish lilac, the sort of color that sits on the edge between a purple and a neutral.
Dull Orange is a muted, earthy orange, a descriptive name more than a historical one.
Dull Purple is a muted reddish purple; the name is a plain modifier, and the books use the phrase for puce and for what happens when painters mix red, yellow and blue.
Dull Red is a descriptive name, a red with the shine taken out, and the books use it as a plain adjective phrase more than as the name of any one dye or pigment.
Dull yellow is a plain description rather than a historic name: a yellow with its brightness turned down, the kind of yellow that weld, buckthorn lake and ochre gave painters.
Dusk is the dim time after sunset, and as a color it is a muted blue-violet, a dark with a little blue left in it.
Dusky Pink is a muted, slightly bluish rose, a long-running name for pinks that have lost their brightness.
Dust is a dull greyish yellow-brown, the colour of dry earth on a surface, and the clearest case of the word in colour history is khaki, which means dusty.
Dusty Blue is a soft, greyed mid blue, a descriptive name that fits the faded look of old indigo work clothes.
Dusty Green is a mid green softened with grey, a plain descriptive name that appears in several color standards without a story of its own.
Dusty Pink is a muted, slightly bluish rose; the word *dusty* means a color with grey mixed in, and the name sits beside old rose and antique pink.
Dutch Blue is a soft grey-blue, a name that has meant different things to dictionaries and to pigment makers.

Earth is the color of bare ground, a mid brown with an orange cast, and the name painters give to the oldest, cheapest and steadiest family of pigments: the ochres, siennas, umbers and green clays dug straight from the soil.
Ebony is the name of a dense tropical heartwood and, from it, of a glossy black; the swatch on screen is a dark green-grey, which is a good reason to read what the books say about the wood.
Ecru is the pale warm off-white of cloth that has not been bleached or dyed, a French word that for centuries stood for what most white things really looked like.
Eggplant is a dark greyish purple named for the fruit of *Solanum melongena*, which British English calls the aubergine.
Eggshell Blue is a very pale, cool blue-green named for a bird's eggshell; as a screen swatch it reads as a minty near-white.

Egyptian blue is a calcium copper silicate, fired from sand, lime and copper in Egypt some 4,500 years ago: among the oldest synthetic pigments, and the standard blue of the ancient Mediterranean for more than two thousand years.
Electric blue is a bright, saturated blue tied to the glow of electrical discharge; the name was in fashion shops by the 1870s, as a dusty periwinkle, long before it became the color of the future.

Emerald green is a brilliant cool green that began as the color of a gem and, from 1814, became the name of a copper-and-arsenic paint that colored Victorian wallpaper, Impressionist canvases and a famous poisoning rumor.
Emerald is a bright, slightly bluish green named after the gem, a beryl tinted by a trace of chromium, and it also names one of the most brilliant and most poisonous paints of the nineteenth century.
Emeraude is French for emerald, and as a color name it points less at the gem than at a green that French and English painters argued over.
Eminence is a deep purple, a dictionary name from the Maerz and Paul era whose meaning of rank and distinction is the only story our books support.
Empire Green is a dark, grey-leaning green tied to Napoleonic France, though Napoleon did not start the fashion.
English red is the old trade name for a red iron-oxide pigment, made by heating yellow ochre or iron sulfate, and it never meant one exact recipe or one place of making.
Espresso is a very dark, reddish brown named for the coffee drink, close to black at a glance and warmer once it sits beside black.
Ether is a medium, slightly greenish blue recorded in the Maerz and Paul color dictionary of 1930; no book we hold says who chose the name.
Eton Blue is a school color: the light blue of Eton, a public school in England, whose name was later shared with a university.
Eucalyptus is a muted grey-green, named in a 1930 color dictionary for the tree.
Evergreen is a dark forest green named for trees that keep their leaves, recorded in color dictionaries since 1915.

Faience is the glazed blue-green ceramic of ancient Egypt, a material that may have helped start glassmaking; the same word later named tin-glazed European earthenware, and a mid blue in a 1930 color dictionary.
Falcon is a dark brown, listed in a 1930 color dictionary under the name of the bird.
Fawn is the light brown of a young deer's coat, a name that sits in Ridgway's 1886 nomenclature and in a 1535 list of pleasing color pairs.
Fawn is a light yellowish brown named for the coat of a young deer, and Renaissance color writers had a lot to say about it.
Fern is a clear mid-bright leaf green, and an irony of dye history: ferns were among the plants northern Europeans used to dye green, yet gave weak, unstable results.
Ferruginous means rust-colored, from the Latin for rust, and describes the reddish brown of iron-bearing earths and stones.
Finn is a deep purple whose name has no documented origin in our sources; it is a color we can measure but cannot yet explain.
Fir Green is a dark, muted green whose name points to the fir tree, a descriptive name with no recorded inventor.
Fire Engine Red is a bright, vivid red, a descriptive name that points to the red of fire engines.
Flame is a vivid reddish orange named for fire, though real flames are rarely this red, and in the pigment books the word names a black.
Flat Blue is an old dyer's grade of indigo, a middle-light blue on a ladder that ran from milk blue to navy, and also a Chinese name for the best azurite.
Flax-flower blue is a soft, slightly purplish blue, number 30 among the blues of Werner's nomenclature of colors, where it is tied to a butterfly, the flax flower and a blue copper ore.
Flesh color is the old name for a warm, pale pink-orange, the shade painters and tailors once used for light skin.
Flesh Pink is a pale pinkish beige, a name from the old habit of describing colors by skin.

Flesh red is a pinkish red from the colour charts of natural history, where Patrick Syme's edition of Werner's nomenclature named human skin, larkspur petals and baryte as its examples; on screens its swatch has aged into a pale peach.
Flirt is a deep purplish red, a name our library traces to the early twentieth-century color dictionaries rather than to any dye or flower.
Floral White is a computer color name: one of the 140 colors in the X11 set, a white with a faint warm tint.
Fontainebleau is a light brownish grey, listed in Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary under the name of the French royal court town and palace.
Forest green is a strong, mid-dark green named for woodland; as a screen color it is the web's ForestGreen, and the name itself was already in English use by 1810.
Foxglove is a medium purple named for the flower, though the books say more about the plant's role in green dyeing.
France Rose is a medium rose pink with a purple cast, known from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, where it is printed on plate 1.
Freedom is a deep blue with a slight violet lean, a color name from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary that no book in our shelf discusses as a color.
French Beige is a light-brown shade-name, one of a long run of "French" colors in the dictionaries, with no recorded story of its own.
French Blue is a strong blue with three histories: the blue of France's royal arms and flag, a name for artificial ultramarine, and a famous stolen diamond.
French green is a muted, slightly yellowish green that the dictionaries file under a country adjective, and that the paint trade used for an altogether different thing.
French grey is a pale, almost neutral grey that English first met as a naturalist's term: Patrick Syme put it on his 1814 color chart, and a young Charles Darwin used it for an octopus.
French White is a pale, greyish pink-lilac in the 1930 Maerz and Paul dictionary, and also an older name from the paint trade for a fine lead white.
Frostbite is a hot, bluish pink, a Crayola-list name whose swatch has little to do with the medical condition it is named for.
Fulvous is an old word for a dull orange or reddish-yellow, used above all for animal colors, especially bird plumage.
Fuscous is a dark, dull, greenish-brown grey, from a Latin root for brown and dusky, kept alive in Ridgway's color nomenclature.

Gallstone Yellow is a deep, brownish yellow named for the stones of the gall bladder, both as number 69 in a nineteenth-century color chart for naturalists and as an artists' pigment ground from the gallstones of oxen.
Gamboge is the bright, slightly lemony yellow of a Southeast Asian tree resin, named for Cambodia, a watercolor of the East India trade and, in 1908, part of the evidence that atoms exist.
Genoa Blue is a muted greenish blue in Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary; the name points to Genoa, the port whose cloth gave the world the word jeans.
Gentian Blue is a strong purplish blue named for the gentian flower, listed by Ridgway in 1912 and the ISCC-NBS in 1955.
Ghost White is a computer color name from the X11 set: a white tipped faintly toward blue.
Glacier is a dark, greyish blue-violet that appears in Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, whose origin the sources do not explain.
Glaucous is an old botanical and literary word for a dull, grey-tinged blue-green, which the charts and the web later pinned to a clearer, bluer swatch.
Gold is the warm, bright yellow of the precious metal, the color that stood in for heaven on medieval altarpieces and for wealth everywhere else, and the one color a screen can only imitate.
Golden brown is a rich yellowy brown, a name Paterson links to hair and to the lichen called crottle.
Golden yellow is a descriptive name for a warm, bright yellow, and across the centuries it has been attached to pigments, dyes and chemicals that share little beyond the adjective.
Goldenrod is the strong, slightly mustardy yellow of the flower of that name, and today it is best known as one of the 140 named colors of the web.
Gooseberry is a dark reddish purple from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary; the name is stranger than the fruit, since the common gooseberry colour name is a green.
Grape is a dark reddish purple named after the fruit, though the books agree that the color is richer than real grapes and that the pigment called grape black is not purple at all.
Grapefruit is a bright coral red, named for the fruit's flush; the books read say little about it, so its history is mostly the library's record.
Graphite Grey is a dark, slightly blue-tinged grey named for the soft carbon of pencils, a mineral that contains no lead.
Graphite is the dark metallic grey of the soft carbon mineral inside a pencil, long mistaken for lead and named for writing.
Grass Green is a green named for turf: a yellowish green that Werner's mineral color table fixed as number 54, and that screens now show far brighter than any historical swatch.
Grass is the green of a lawn in the sun, but the older color books meant a quieter green by the name, and painters struggled for centuries to make it at all.
Grebe is a dark, warm grey with a brownish cast, named for the plumage of the diving water bird.
Green-Blue is a descriptive name, not a story: the slot between green and blue on a painter's color wheel, a standard color name, and a label that three sources attach to three different colors.
Green Brown is a plain descriptive name for a dull olive-khaki; as a swatch it is RAL 8000, a paint standard, and the books say little about it as a color.
Green earth is a pale, greyish green clay pigment, a mixture of celadonite or glauconite, that painters dug from Cyprus to Verona and laid under flesh for two thousand years.
Green grey is a descriptive name for a muted green with a good deal of grey in it; it is not a pigment or a dye, and the books use the phrase for many different things.
Green Yellow is the electric yellow-green of the web keyword `greenyellow`, a name that sits on a border which older European color orders refused to draw: a yellow that leans toward green.

Green is the color of leaves and grass, everywhere in nature yet hard for people to make or keep: for centuries an unstable color of youth, love, chance and poison, and today the color of nature itself.
Greenish Black is one of the named blacks in Werner's nomenclature of colors, the mineralogist's vocabulary of the 1770s, and its swatch on a screen is a neutral dark grey with no green in it at all.

Greenish blue is a blue leaning toward green: an old descriptive phrase that Abraham Werner's mineral colors turned into a fixed name, and that dictionaries still use for everything from peacock feathers to a pale winter horizon.
Greenish Grey is a grey with a faint green cast, a name from the mineralogists' color charts of the 1790s that Syme fixed as number 15 in his 1821 edition of Werner's *Nomenclature of Colours*.
Greenish white is the sixth white in Werner's colour chart, a snow white with a trace of green, shown on a goldcrest's feathers, a narcissus petal and a lump of calc sinter.
Greenish yellow is a yellow tipped toward green, a color that Europeans have long found hard to like and that mineralogists, dyers and pigment makers have each had to name.
Grey Beige is a light, greyed tan, the color of undyed wool and dry dust, named by blending two neutral words.
Grey Blue is a muted, slightly greenish sky blue, a plain name built from two colour words that most traditions have used for a very long time without ever fixing it to one pigment.
Grey brown is a name for a dull, warm neutral, and it has meant two quite different swatches: a mid olive-tinged brown on screens today and a near-black in older charts.
Grey green is a descriptive name for a muted green, best known in the books through celadon, the pale Chinese glaze, and through the way distance dulls foliage.
Grey Olive is a very dark, greyed olive, a name our library files under a Japanese traditional color and an early German standard.
Grey pink is a descriptive color name, a pink greyed down until it is dusty, and it has more to say about how we name colors than about any one history.
Grey Purple is a muted, dusty violet, a plain descriptive name that several color systems recorded long before screens did.
Grey white is a pale warm off-white, and in our data a paint-industry name from the RAL system.

Grey is the color between black and white, the one color that is named after nothing; it has meant poverty, hope, old age and good taste in turn, and it changes its look more readily than any other color.
Greyish black is a black softened with grey, a name that appears as number 17 among the blacks in Patrick Syme's 1821 edition of the mineralogist Werner's color list.
Greyish blue is a blue dulled with grey: the name Patrick Syme gave in 1821 to a mineralogist's smalt blue, later the color French soldiers wore into 1915, and the quiet blue of harbor skies.
Greyish brown is a plain descriptive name for a muted, earthy brown, and it is one of the most common colors in the paintings we have measured.

Greyish green is a descriptive phrase, not a named color: a green with the brightness taken out, which the books reach for whenever they need to say that something looks dull, aged, military or quiet.
Greyish White is a color from the age of Werner's mineralogy: the eighth white on Syme's chart, defined as snow white with a touch of ash grey and illustrated with a kittiwake's feathers.

Gull is an old English word for a shade of grey, now shown as a grayish olive; the books say little about it, but one nineteenth-century color chart took several of its whites and greys from gull feathers.
Gunmetal is the dark blue-grey of the alloy once used for cannon and gun parts, and it is now a standard word for a cool, dark grey.
Haematite Red is a dark, greyed brownish red, the color of iron ore and of the oldest red earth pigment.
Hair Brown is a grey-tinged, olive-leaning brown from the mineralogists' color lists of around 1800, defined then by a bird's head and a tin ore and later worn as a fashionable color.
Harvest Gold is a deep, saturated orange-yellow, the color of ripe grain and, to a generation, of 1970s kitchens.
Hazel is named for the hazelnut and the shrub it grows on; Paterson files it among the browns, while this screen swatch is a darker, greener gold.
Heat Wave is a vivid, fully saturated orange, a name from the modern lists of fashion and crayon shades, with no recorded author or date.
Heather is the dusty purple of the moorland shrub's flowers, a muted mauve-grey that is more a texture than a single hue.
Heliotrope is a purple named for a flowering shrub, famous in late Victorian fashion for its bright combinations, its place in mourning dress and its appearance on stage in Oscar Wilde.
Honey yellow is a name from Werner's nineteenth-century colour list for minerals and animals, painted as a brownish gold by Patrick Syme in 1821.
Honeydew is a very pale green, a web-standard color name that shares a word with the melon, the sweet insect secretion, and an older pinkish tint.
Hot Magenta is a fluorescent-bright pink-violet, the color of 1970s punk lettering and the Crayola fluorescent box.

Hot pink is an intensely saturated pink; a color Paterson calls particularly popular in the 1950s, close kin to Schiaparelli's shocking pink of 1937, and fixed on screens as one of the 140 X11 colors.
Hunter green is a dark, slightly yellowish green, the kind of color a dictionary file puts near Hooker's and Lincoln green.
Hyacinth blue is a deep purplish blue named for the flower, and its older echo, the biblical hyacinth blue, was a shade of cloth that stood beside scarlet and purple.
Hyacinth Red is the orange-red of the gem once called hyacinth, set down as number 83 in the English version of Werner's nomenclature of colors and used by Darwin on the Beagle.
Hyacinth Violet is a deep, reddish purple, named for the color of the flower in its purple form.
Hydrangea Pink is named for the flower, a soft pink with a hint of yellow, and for a plant whose color is famously unsteady.
Hydrangea Red is a muted, greyed red, the color of the flower heads when they take on a reddish tone.
Hydro is a muted grey-green from the 1930 Maerz and Paul dictionary, first recorded in 1920, and none of the color books we hold explains the name.
Ice is a very pale cool tint, between blue and green: the color of light scattered inside snow and ice, and a name that painters, dyers and dictionaries have used in different ways.
Iceberg is a clear light blue that entered the color charts in the 1920s and 1930s; the books have almost nothing to say about it as a color.
Imperial Blue is a deep blue with a grand name, part of a small family of colors that borrowed "imperial" from the yellow of the Chinese court.
Imperial green is a nineteenth-century name for a copper-arsenic green related to emerald green, and today's swatch is a clean mid green far brighter than the dull pigment the trade manuals describe.

Imperial purple was the shellfish dye of Rome and Byzantium, so costly that emperors fenced it with law; the muted blue-violet that carries its name on screen comes from a nineteenth-century mineralogist's color chart, not from the dye.
Imperial red is a strong, slightly bluish red whose name has pointed at an old court color, a pigment lake and the modern screen swatch.

Imperial is a deep plum-violet named for imperial purple, the shellfish dye that Roman and Byzantine emperors kept for themselves; the word was later lent to blues, reds, yellows and greens that wanted the same majesty.
Inde blue is an old dictionary color name for a dark, greyish purple, despite the word blue in it.
Independence is a dark, dusty blue-violet whose name no color book explains.
Indian lake is an old name for a red lake pigment made from lac, the resin of an Asian scale insect; as a screen color it is a dull, greyish purplish red.
Indian red is an old pigment of finely ground iron oxide, a dark brownish red; the web color that borrows its name is a much lighter, pinker red.

Indian yellow is a deep, glowing golden yellow watercolor pigment that came from India in hard, foul-smelling balls, and its reputed source, the urine of mango-fed cows, is one of the best-known stories in the history of color, and one of the shakiest.
Indigo Blue is a mid greyish blue with three lives: the name of the dye's own colorant, a numbered entry in Werner's mineral color chart, and the everyday blue of denim.
Indigo dye is the deep, greyed blue made from the leaves of many plants, and the only major natural dye that works by being dissolved colorless and then turning blue in the air.

Indigo is two colors with one name: the deep, greyed blue of the oldest blue dye on earth, and the violet-blue band Newton squeezed into the rainbow. In Japan the dye is *ai*, and its blues have their own names.
Invisible green is a very dark green, named for how close it sits to black.
Iris is the blue-violet of the flower named for the Greek rainbow goddess; in the Middle Ages the same plant also gave painters a green, which is stranger than it sounds.
Irresistible is a deep rose-crimson with a name that reads like a sales pitch; no book read uses it as a color, and its history is that of the shades around it.
Isabella Color is a dark, greyish yellow-tan, a swatch from Ridgway's atlases of 1886 and 1912.
Isabelline is a pale, faintly yellowish grey-white, an old name for the color of undyed linen and of pale dun animals, saddled with one of color history's most persistent bad jokes.
Ivory is the off-white of an elephant's tusk, a color named for a material so prized that it gave us chessmen, bridal satin, a black pigment and a long trade in white gold.
Ivy green is a dark, muted olive green named for the leaves of ivy, and it is a surprisingly common color in painting.
Jade green is a green named for the stone, and Paterson's definition spans blue-green to yellowish green.
Jade is a green named for a stone, and the stone is really two unrelated minerals; the word came into English from a Spanish phrase for the flank, because the rock was once worn against kidney pain.
Japonica is a dusty rose-mauve from the Maerz and Paul color dictionary of 1930, named with the Latin word for 'of Japan'.
Jet is a black gemstone made from fossilized wood, a hard, polishable lignite that Queen Victoria's long mourning turned into the color of grief and the livelihood of a Yorkshire fishing town.
Jungle green is a modern name for a cool green; the name's definition and this swatch do not quite agree.
Kashmir is a dark, muted green named for the Himalayan valley; nothing in the books explains why, though the place is famous for shawls, saffron and sapphires.
Kelly green is the bright spring-grass green worn on St. Patrick's Day, a color named for an Irish surname and, by one account, only a century old.
Khaki Brown is a dark olive-brown, named from the dust-colored cloth of army uniforms.
Khaki is a drab, dust-colored brownish yellow-green, named from an Indian-language word for dust, and the color that moved armies out of bright uniforms into ones meant to be hard to see.
Kobe is a deep brick-brown red from the color charts of the 1920s, and nothing in our books explains its name.
Kremlin is a deep blue-green from the Maerz and Paul dictionary of color, a name that has nothing to do with the walls it recalls.
Lapis lazuli is the deep blue stone of Afghanistan, flecked with pyrite, that medieval painters turned into the most expensive pigment in Europe, ultramarine.
Lavender Blue is a pale, slightly violet blue named for the flower, and an old entry in the systems naturalists used to describe butterflies, flowers and stones.
Lavender Blush is an almost-white pink, one of the 140 named colors of the X11 set that web browsers adopted as CSS keywords.
Lavender grey is a pale, cool grey with a trace of purple, named for the color of lavender flowers.

Lavender Purple is the name of one of the colors in the old nomenclature of Werner, a mineralogist's scheme of the 1700s, where it is a bluish purple matched to dried lavender flowers, a butterfly's wing and a stone.
Lavender is the pale bluish purple of lavender flowers, a color word English has used since the early 1700s, and a name that has been pinned to several quite different swatches since.
Leaf green is the yellowish green of young leaves, and also, in the pigment trade, an old name for a durable pale green made from chromium.
Leaf is a fresh, strong yellow-green, the color a young leaf shows against the light; the same word in older color lists names the brown of a dead one.
Leather is the color of tanned hide, a mid orange-brown named for a material that has been dyed nearly every other color, from Egyptian canopies stained blue to Charlemagne's scarlet shoes.
Leek green is the greyed, yellowish green of the leek's leaf; the Greeks built a word for green on it, Davy named chlorine for it, and Werner's mineral chart made it number 48.
Leghorn is the pale yellow of bleached straw, named for the Italian port that gave its name to a famous straw hat.
Lemon yellow is a bright, cool yellow named for the fruit, and as a paint it was a family of nineteenth-century chromium and cadmium pigments sold under one name.
Lettuce green is a soft yellowish green named for lettuce leaves, with a long record in color dictionaries.
Levant red is an alternative name for Turkey red, a brilliant alizarin red dye used in Britain from 1785 into the 1930s.
Liberty is a mid blue-violet that has a place in three color lists and in none of the color books; its name has no documented story, while the idea it names has been given red, green, buff and blue.
Lichen green is a very pale, cool green, named for the whitish green of lichen.
Light blue is the plain name for a pale blue, and it points at a different swatch in almost every standard; its real history is in who could wear it, what it cost to dye, and how it behaves at dusk.
Light brown is a plain description rather than a historic color name, and old color dictionaries use it as a gloss for dozens of earthy names from ochre to biscuit.
Light Cadmium is a warm, slightly dull gold, named after cadmium yellow light, the pale end of the cadmium sulfide pigments.
Light coral is a web color, a soft pinkish red from the X11 set, defined by its hex code rather than a long history.
Light Cyan is a very pale aqua tint, a CSS and X11 keyword whose parent word, cyan, is a primary of printing.

Light Green is the web's pale, fresh green, one of the X11 colors; the words "light green" are far older than the screen, and across the books they mark a green that is young, cheerful and easy on the eye.
Light Grey Green is a descriptive name for a pale, softly greyed spring green, and it has been in color charts since 1912.
Light Grey is the pale neutral that web designers know as `lightgrey`, and a plain descriptive name that the books use for mourning cloth, Vermeer's walls and overcast skies.
Light Lavender is a very pale violet, a lightened lavender, and as a painted color it is almost absent from the museum record.
Light Olive is a descriptive name for a pale olive, and the books show it in an old color-chart skin description and as part of a paint name.
Light orange is a descriptive name for a pale, warm orange; the books mostly use it as a plain description rather than a named color.
Light Pink is the web's name for a pale, slightly warm pink, one of the 140 colors in the X11 set and later in CSS, with the hex code #FFB6C1.
Light Red is a painter's name for the brownish red made by burning yellow ochre, and also a plain description of a bright red; the screen swatch here is the second, not the first.
Light salmon is a web color, a soft pinkish orange from the X11 set named as a lighter salmon.
Light sea green is a web color, a cool teal-green from the X11 set, that is actually fairly dark for a name that says light.
Light Slate Grey is a cool, bluish grey that is a named color in CSS, with the spelling gray or grey both accepted in the web names.
Light Tan is a pale cream-yellow on screens, much lighter than the leather tan its name suggests, and it has a family of older names.
Light Violet is a soft blue-violet whose name has meant different colors on different charts; on one survey it is a pale pink-lilac instead.
Light yellow is a descriptive name for a very pale yellow, best known today as an entry in the web's X11 color list, and in older books a loose label for pale yellow pigments, dyes and fabrics.
Lilac-Grey is a pale, warm-leaning light grey with only a whisper of violet, a name carried over from Ridgway's color nomenclature.
Lilac is the pale, slightly pinkish purple of the lilac blossom, a word with a dark blue ancestor that was the common-speech name for the first mass-market purple dye.
Lily green is a pale yellow-green with two lives: a rarely used name in color dictionaries, and a medieval flower pigment that probably came from iris, not lilies.
Lime green is a vivid, slightly yellowish green; on the web it is X11's #32CD32, while the older paint of the same name was a copper-and-arsenic green thinned with a white calcium filler.
Lime Yellow is a vivid, green-leaning yellow, bright enough to sit on the border between yellow and green.
Lime is the yellowish green of the lime fruit, and the same word names the white caustic mineral that coated walls, set fresco and sat in dye vats for centuries.
Linen is the pale, faintly pink off-white of the X11 color set, named for cloth woven from flax, the oldest textile known, whose natural color is greyer and browner than its name suggests.
Lint is a muted, yellowish tan from the fashion color cards of the early twentieth century.
Lion is a pale sandy yellow, named for the coat of the animal and recorded as a color name by Maerz and Paul in 1930.
Lipstick Red is a strong, slightly blue red, a name that reads as ordinary language but has no documented origin.
Lipstick is a deep pink-red named for a cosmetic, and the cosmetic's own reds have come from cinnabar, from cochineal insects and from the laboratory.
Liver Brown is a dark, slightly reddish brown that comes straight out of the mineralogists' colour list, where it was defined as a recipe: chestnut brown darkened with a little black and olive green.
Liver is a dark, greyed reddish brown named for the organ, a color that ancient doctors used to describe a red earth and eighteenth-century naturalists used to rank browns.
Lumiere Blue is a pale grey-green teal on screens, and its name echoes an obscure artificial pigment, bleu lumière, listed in 1901.
Madder Blue is a greyish violet-blue named in Ridgway's atlas, and a puzzle: madder gives reds, and our sources do not say why a blue carries its name.
Madder brown is a reddish brown named for the madder root: a nineteenth-century artist's pigment made by gently heating madder lake until it turned from red to brown.
Madder lake is the painter's form of the madder root: its red dye fixed on a colorless base, sold in grades from deep carmine to pale rose, loved for its glow and blamed for its fading.
Madder Violet is a deep, reddish purple named for the dye plant that gives madder red, and a color that old dyers and color chartmakers recognized as one of madder's side effects.
Madder is the red of a root: probably the oldest dye people ever made, the secret behind Turkey red and rose madder, and the first natural dye ever rebuilt in a laboratory.

Magenta is the red-purple of the first magenta dye, a coal-tar color made in France in 1858 or 1859 and named for a battle in Italy; on screens and in printing it is now the pure pink-purple where red and blue light meet.
Mahogany Brown is a very dark reddish brown named for polished mahogany wood, and it is also the paint standard RAL 8016.
Mahogany Red is a warm red-brown named for the hardwood, and Maerz and Paul's dictionary dates it to 1843.
Mahogany is the dark reddish brown of polished mahogany wood, a name that furniture makers, dyers and painters' colormen all borrowed.
Maize is a bright, warm yellow named for the ripe kernels of the American grain that English calls corn.

Malachite green is the green of the copper mineral malachite, which painters ground into pigment for thousands of years; the same name was later given to a coal-tar dye, so it points at several different materials.
Malachite is a banded green copper mineral, ground as a pigment since ancient Egypt and named for the mallow leaf, that gave its name to a vivid green on screens and to a family of later greens.
Mallow Red is a muted, purplish crimson named for the mallow flower, close kin to mauve.
Mandarin Orange is a deep, reddish orange named for the fruit; a dictionary calls the name a reddish yellow, and the exact tone has drifted.
Mandarin is a vivid reddish orange named for the mandarin fruit, a word that also names Chinese officials, a garnet and a style of robe, and the books do not agree on which exact orange it is.
Manganese Violet is a muted red-violet that takes its name from a nineteenth-century artists' pigment, introduced in 1868 as a safer replacement for cobalt violet.
Manila is a light yellowish brown, a color name Maerz and Paul date to 1892 and shared with the Philippine capital.
Mantis is a fresh, light leaf green; the books say nothing about it as a color, but they have a lot to say about the animals that share the name.
Maple is an orangey-yellow, and the tree behind the name gives painters, violin makers and dyers three very different stories.
Marie Antoinette is a dusty pink-brown named for the last queen of the old French monarchy; the name entered the Maerz and Paul dictionary in 1926, long after her death.

Marigold is the warm orange-yellow of the garden flower, a color that naturalists once used as a standard for orange, that a pigment maker used as a shade name, and that got a Nuremberg saffron dealer burned for fraud in 1444, according to one book.
Marine Blue is a dark, slightly greenish blue of the sea; the one dictionary that defines it ties it to a military uniform.
Marine is a very dark blue, close to navy, whose name is the French bleu marine in English clothes; its best-documented career is as the color that replaced black in uniforms.
Maroon is a dark brownish red, named from the French word for the chestnut, and it began as a brown before it became a red.
Mars orange is a reddish orange paint made synthetically from iron oxide, one of a family of eighteenth-century pigments named for the alchemists' planet-metal Mars.
Mascot is a very dark navy blue from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, and the reason for its name is undocumented.
Massicot is a yellow oxide of lead, one of the oldest painters' yellows, and a pale, creamy one on screen.
Mauve is the French name of the mallow flower, borrowed for a soft greyish purple; in 1856 an 18-year-old chemist made a coal-tar dye that took the name and turned it into a craze.
Mauvette is a very pale, pinkish lilac, a diminutive cousin of mauve.
May Green is a mid, slightly yellowish green, the name RAL gave to its standard color 6017, and one that a pigment reference files as a rare variant name for emerald green.
Mazarine Blue is an old name for a rich blue, possibly honoring a French cardinal; the modern swatch is much lighter than the word suggests.
Meadow is a dark, slightly yellowish green named for hay-and-grass country, a word that mineralogists, pigment makers and painters each used in their own way.
Medium Aquamarine is a soft sea-green from the named colors of the web.
Medium Blue is a pure, saturated blue, one of the named colors of the web.
Medium Orchid is a bright, blue-leaning violet-pink, one of the named colors of the web.
Medium Pink is a saturated, slightly bluish pink, a plain descriptive name that a 2010 online color survey put on the map and that no color book treats as a color of its own.
Medium Purple is a soft, blue-leaning purple from the named colors of the web.
Medium Slate Blue is a bright, electric blue-violet that exists as a color name because it sits in the X11 color list and, from there, in the CSS color keywords.
Medium Turquoise is a clear blue-green from the X11 and CSS color lists, a neighbor of turquoise.
Melon is a pale, warm pink with a touch of orange, named for the flesh of a ripe fruit and recorded as a color name since at least 1892.
Metallic Blue is a grayish steel blue named by an online color survey, borrowing the vocabulary of car paint for a color that is flat on a screen.
