Metallic Gold is a warm yellow, a flat screen stand-in for the look of the metal itself.

Metallic Green is a dark olive from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary; despite the name, the swatch is closer to olive brown than to green, and the copper greens that painters called metallic are a different thing.
Michigan is a deep teal green-blue from the Maerz and Paul dictionary; the books say nothing about why it carries a state's name.
Middle grey is the grey halfway between black and white, a reference that painters and designers use to judge every other color.

Midnight blue is the blue of the sky at its darkest, a deep violet-leaning navy that Paterson's dictionary says was apparently the correct shade for men's evening dress, before it became a crayon, a screen color and a name for oxidized indigo.
Midnight is the color of the sky at its darkest, a name that books use for deep indigo blues, and the swatch here is a near-black navy that few painters ever needed.
Mineral green is a name that colourmen attached to many different green pigments, mostly copper compounds, so it points to a family of recipes and a trade habit more than to one substance.
Mineral Red is a muted brownish red from Ridgway's 1912 color nomenclature, a descriptive name rather than the record of a single pigment.
Ming is a deep, greyed greenish-blue named for the Chinese dynasty and its porcelain, though the porcelain's famous blue was cobalt, a different and more violet color.
Mint Cream is a near-white with the faintest green tint, a screen color from the X11 and CSS lists.
Mint is the pale, cool green of the herb's leaves, a pastel that has come to mean freshness and cleanliness.
Misty Rose is a very pale pink, a screen color from the X11 and CSS lists.
Mocha is a warm, mid-toned coffee brown named for the drink; Paterson's definition is darker than the swatch most people mean.
Mona Lisa is a light, warm pink on web color lists; the name apparently borrows Leonardo's portrait, though the pink it suggests is the one the painting lost.
Montpellier green is a name for verdigris, the green made from copper, taken from the French city that was an important verdigris-making center for several centuries.

Morocco is the color of a leather, a deep brown in the library but a brick red in the one glossary that explains the word, and it is named for a country the color books mostly visit for other reasons.
Moss green is a muted yellowish green named for the plant, and the name has also been used for a pigment whose identity the books cannot agree on.
Moss Grey is a muted greenish grey, a color defined by the old RAL system and the ISCC-NBS names.

Moss is the yellowish, softly greyed green of the plant that carpets stones and trees, a color word that dictionaries define by the plant and paint catalogues borrowed for several different mixed greens.
Mossy Green is a medium, yellowish green that names the color of moss, and the same words turn up in recipes for making a dark green out of old verdigris.
Mosul is a moderate yellowish brown from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, named for the Iraqi city that was once a market for textiles and dye materials.
Mountain green is a pale grey-green from Syme's 1821 color nomenclature, which shares its name with an older pigment word for green copper minerals such as malachite.
Mountbatten pink is a dull, greyed mauve-pink that a British naval officer adopted as ship camouflage in the early Second World War; its fame rests on one tale of a lucky cruiser.
Mud is the color of wet soil, a name that has carried a faint insult for painters and a good deal of practical use for dyers and soldiers.
Mulberry is named for the fruit of the mulberry tree, and for centuries it meant a dark purplish red; on a screen today it is a brighter, pinker magenta.
Mushroom is a pale greyish brown with a warm pink cast, named plainly for the vegetable.
Musk is a dark, warm brown named for the strong-smelling secretion of the male musk deer, and the dictionaries date the color name to 1654.
Mustard Brown is a deep, brownish yellow named for prepared mustard, recorded in color charts by the 1920s.
Mustard yellow is the deep, slightly warm yellow of the table condiment, a name that grew out of the shorter word mustard.
Mustard is the deep yellow of the condiment, a color that eighteenth-century France briefly adored and Europeans have mostly distrusted since.
Myrtle Green is a dark bluish green named for the leaf of the myrtle shrub, recorded in color charts since Ridgway's 1886 nomenclature.
Naiad is a soft, light green from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, named for the water nymphs of Greek myth.
Navy is a dark, slightly greyed blue named for naval uniforms, which were dyed with indigo; in the twentieth century it replaced black as the color of work uniforms and men's suits.
Near black is a black with a trace of color in it, which is how some painters, from Gauguin on, made their darkest darks.
Neon Red is an extremely saturated red, named for the glow of a neon tube, and a good example of a color no tube of paint and no flat screen swatch can fully reproduce.
Nickel is a neutral mid grey named for the metal; the books say little about the grey itself, but a good deal about nickel's greens, yellows and one famous black.
Nile Blue is a pale, soft blue-green with a name taken from the river, recorded in color charts since the 1880s.
Nuremberg violet is an old trade name for manganese violet, a purple pigment made from manganese phosphates and introduced in 1868.
Nut brown is the brown of nuts, in practice a warm reddish brown; it is among the most common browns in our painting archive.
Nutmeg is a medium-dark brown named for the spice, a color Shakespeare already used in a line of Henry V.
Oatmeal is a pale, warm grey-beige named for the food, and a color that old dictionaries and modern standards describe from opposite sides.
Ocean Green is a clear, medium sea-green, and one of the few color names whose dictionary definition does not match its own standard swatch.
Ocean is a deep blue-green, the color the word suggests today; for most of European history, though, water was painted green, and the sea took a long time to become blue.
Ocher red is the red of iron oxide earth: the oldest pigment family, dug from the ground or made by roasting yellow ochre, and used in painting for a very long time.
Ochre brown is the brown of iron-rich earth, a deep golden-brown named for ochre, the clay that iron oxide colors.

Ochre Yellow is the pale golden yellow that Werner's nineteenth-century color chart matched to a bird's feathers and a polished stone, named for yellow ochre, the iron-rich earth that painters have dug for pigment since the Palaeolithic.

Ochre is iron in the ground: a family of yellow, orange and red earths that people have dug, washed and burned for paint longer than any other pigment, and that still sits in nearly every painter's box.
Oil Green is number 60 in Patrick Syme's 1821 chart of colors for naturalists, an olive gold that he pinned to a water snail's shell, an apple's skin and a beryl.
Old gold is a glossy yellow, named by comparison with the metal; Paterson dates it as a color term to 1879.
Old rose is a muted, dusty pink, the color of a faded rose rather than a fresh one.
Olive-Brown is a muted greenish brown, the color of a kestrel's head and a blackcurrant stem in an Edinburgh flower-painter's 1821 chart, and of a quarter of the paintings in our archive.
Olive green is the dull yellow-green of unripe olives. On today's screens it is a light yellow-green, but in old charts, paint boxes and uniforms it meant something darker and browner.
Olive-grey is a green shade of grey, also called Scotch grey, and named for the olive.
Olive is a dull, brownish green named for the olive tree and its fruit; on screens it is a bright yellow-green, while the charts of the past kept it far browner and greyer.
Opal is the pale, milky grey-green of a stone famous for the opposite: a gem whose own color is a shifting play of flashes, and whose name as a plain color means something quiet and uncertain.
Orange brown is a plain description for a mid-dark brown that leans toward orange, the hue of burnt iron earths, dead bracken and the tawny of a dry leaf.
Orange Peel is a vivid, warm orange-yellow named for the fruit's skin, a color of signs and screens more than of paint.
Orange red is the zone where red tips toward orange, and the web color #FF4500 sits in the middle of it; its history is the history of the pigments and dyes that lived there.

Orange is the color between red and yellow, named after a fruit: a late arrival as a word, a pigment and an idea, which went on to become the color of princes, monks' robes and every warning sign that needs to be seen.
Orchid Pink is a soft, light pink with a hint of purple, named for the flower and easy to confuse with the much stronger web color Orchid.
Orchid is a light, slightly pink violet, best known today as one of the 140 named colors of the web, and its title comes from the flower rather than from any pigment.
Orpiment Orange is a warm orange from Patrick Syme's 1821 color chart, named for the arsenic mineral orpiment even though true orpiment is mostly yellow.

Orpiment is the bright, slightly lemony yellow of an arsenic mineral: its Latin name means gold paint, it gave the world the word arsenic, and for more than three thousand years painters used it as gold's stand-in while trying not to poison themselves.
Oxblood is a very dark, slightly brownish red, named for the color of ox blood.
Oxford blue is a very dark blue named for the University of Oxford, whose sporting color it is.
Oxheart is a deep, brownish red named for the meat, a cousin of oxblood that the dictionaries file simply as deep red.
Oyster Grey is a pale grey tinged with green and yellow, named for the mollusc, and again a name whose dictionary gloss runs brown.
Pale Blue-Green is a descriptive phrase more than a name, a very light green that the books use for pigments and the standards use for a swatch.
Pale brown is a descriptive phrase more than a name: Paterson and St Clair use it to define caramel, cognac, dust and café au lait.
Pale Cerulean is a light, soft sky blue, a lightened step of [[cerulean]].
Pale Goldenrod is the web color #EEE8AA, a pale, slightly greenish yellow named for a washed-out version of the goldenrod flower.
Pale grey is a descriptive phrase for a grey close to white, and the swatch here is nearly paper white; the interest is in how books use the words.
Pale Greyish Blue is a light blue with a touch of grey, the kind of color dictionaries describe rather than name.
Pale Lavender is a very light, slightly pink violet, a descriptive name that two color systems list and a few writers use mostly as a mood.
Pale Lilac is a faint, greyed pink-purple, a color Ball uses to show how Rembrandt could make a violet tint without any blue.
Pale Lime is a soft, light yellow-green; as a color name it is simply descriptive, and the books we hold say almost nothing about it.
Pale Mauve is a light, soft lilac-purple, the faded end of [[mauve]]'s long fashion career.
Pale Olive Green is a light, yellowish green, the color of young olive leaves and some copper minerals.
Pale olive is a light, yellowish green, the color name used for soft olive tones rather than the dark olive of the fruit.
Pale Orange-Yellow is a light, warm yellow tipped with orange, a descriptive name more than a historical one.
Pale Orange is a light, soft orange, closer to a sherbet than to a fruit.
Pale Peach is a light, creamy pink-orange, the color of a peach's skin faded almost to cream.
Pale pink is a very light pink, a rosy tint with much white in it; in painting it can be what is left when a red lake has faded.
Pale purple is a descriptive name: a light, soft purple that dictionaries use to define lilac, thistle and other named shades.
Pale Sky Blue is a very light, slightly greenish blue; on screens it reads almost cyan, while painters have used the phrase for what finely ground azurite looks like.
Pale Turquoise is a light, greenish-blue tint of turquoise, best known as a web color and as the wrong answer to the question of what color the universe is.
Pale Violet Red is a mid pink-red named in the X11 and CSS color lists, where it is written as one word, `palevioletred`.
Pale Violet is a light, clear violet, a descriptive phrase that old books apply to flowers and dyes and that our painting archive does not find at all.
Pale Yellow-Green is a light, soft green leaning to yellow, a systematic name from Ridgway's color plates rather than a pigment or a plant.
Pansy purple is a flower name from the early nineteenth century, one of the purples that the Scottish painter Patrick Syme added when he revised Abraham Werner's color nomenclature.
Pansy is a deep violet-blue named for the flower; the older "pansy purple" was a naturalist's color in Patrick Syme's 1814 chart, and a different shade again.
Parrot green names the vivid yellowish green of a parakeet's plumage, and it was also a nineteenth-century paint name for arsenic-copper greens; the names did not always mean the same compound.
Pastel Blue is a pale, greyed blue; the word pastel names the softness, but it had an older life in French as the name of a blue dye paste made from woad.
Pastel green is a soft, light green, named for its pale chalky look rather than for any one dye or pigment.
Pastel Pink is a pale, softened pink, named by adding "pastel" to pink; the word is a description of lightness, not a pigment.
Patent blue is a deep greenish blue, the name of a blue dye used as a food colouring and in medicine.
Pavonine is an old word for the colors of a peacock: iridescent greenish blue; the Maerz and Paul color dictionary used it for a dull blue.
Peach is the yellowish pink of the fruit's skin, a color word recorded in English by 1588, and the name also belongs to a black pigment made from the fruit's stones.
Peacock blue is the greenish blue of a peacock, a name Paterson defines as greenish blue and one that turns up in Victorian fashion pairings.
Pear is a bright yellow-green named for the fruit; it is a young color name, and the books have almost nothing to say about it as a color.
Pearl grey is a pale, quiet grey, listed as number 12 among the greys of Syme's 1821 color guide for naturalists, where its examples were a gull's back, a flower's petals and a piece of stone.
Pearl is the pale, cool grey of the gem's body color, though real pearls range from white to black, and a pearl's glow comes from layered light, not from pigment.
Pelican is a dark, nearly neutral grey from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary of color, and no book we hold says why it carries a bird's name.
Peony red is a dark red, named for the flower, with a few appearances in textile description.
Peppermint is a fresh mid green, named for the herb and the candy flavor more than for any pigment.
Periwinkle blue is a light purplish blue, the shade named after the periwinkle flower.

Periwinkle is a light, slightly purplish blue named for the flower, and it sits where blue becomes lilac, which is why the books call it purplish blue, lilac-blue and, for one famous suit, argue over whether it is purple at all.
Persian blue is a name two dictionaries use for two different things: a strong blue, and an old trade name for Prussian blue.
Persian Green is a strong blue-green; the name is older than the screen color, since an 1906 formula already used it for a mixed pigment of greens.
Persian orange is a warm, muted orange, a reddish yellow in the old dictionaries, and the clay-and-leather tone of many painted pages.
Persimmon is the reddish orange of the ripe persimmon fruit, and a color name that books also stretch to the red-brown of the tree's wood.
Petrol is a dark blue-green named for the iridescent sheen of petrol on water; petrol is the British word for the fuel.
Petunia is a very dark purple, named for the garden flower.
Phthalo green is a modern synthetic green pigment, deep, cool and intense, first made in the 20th century.
Pinchbeck brown is a brown named for a metal, listed in early nineteenth-century color nomenclatures.
Pine Green is a deep bluish green named after the conifer; the books say almost nothing about it as a color, but one jeweller's note shows where the word shows up in practice: amber.
Pink Coral is a warm, soft pink named for the sea animal's skeleton; as a color name it is a twentieth-century dictionary entry, and the books mention it only in passing.
Pink Lavender is a soft, dusty pink-violet, a descriptive name that the books we hold never discuss as a single color.
Pink Red is a vivid, slightly bluish red-pink from web color lists; the name is a modern compound of two basic color words, and the books treat pink and red as separate colors.

Pink is pale red, the only basic English color word that names part of another one. The ancients saw it but never named it, Europe filed it as a kind of yellow for three centuries, it fades faster than almost any other paint, and it became a girls' color only in the twentieth century.
Pinkish Orange is a modifier name, an orange leaning pink; its one book appearance is a dictionary entry that links the phrase to the padparadscha sapphire.
Pinkish red is the dictionary's all-purpose gloss for a red with a pink cast, used to define lobster, rose, ruby and brick before it was ever a color name of its own.
Pinky Purple is a casual modifier name for a vivid magenta-leaning purple; the only book note is that the word heather now means exactly this.
Pistachio is the pale yellowish green of the nut kernel; it entered the standard color charts of the early 1800s as number 57 of Werner and Syme's greens.
Platinum is the cool, pale grey-white of the metal, a name that moved from a Spanish nickname for a metal thought almost worthless to the jeweller's finest white and the colour of silvery hair.
Plum Purple is a dark, blue-leaning violet whose name was fixed by the painter Patrick Syme, who in 1814 moved Werner's plum blue into a new purple category.
Plum is the reddish purple of a ripe plum's skin, a color word that naturalists were using by the early 1800s and that the web now uses for two quite different colors.
Plunket is an old English word for a greyish blue, once used for common pale blue cloth and now mostly a curiosity.
Pompeian blue is an old name for Egyptian blue, the ancient copper-calcium silicate pigment, and was also borrowed for some weak synthetic lakes.
Pompeian red is a muted brick red named for the walls of Pompeii, and in the pigment trade it was a name for a natural iron-oxide red also sold as Venetian or Indian red.
Popcorn is a warm, pale gold named for the snack, and the color books say almost nothing about it as a color.
Powder blue is a pale, slightly greenish sky blue, and the name is older than the color: it began as a term for powdered smalt, a ground blue glass.
Primary Blue is a vivid, nearly pure screen blue, and a name that points to an old argument about which three colors can make all the rest.

Primrose yellow is a pale, slightly greenish yellow named for the wild primrose; naturalists fixed it in the early 1800s, and paint makers later gave the same name to several unrelated pale chromate pigments.

Prussian blue is a deep, slightly green-leaning blue made by accident in Berlin around 1705: the first cheap, strong blue painters ever had, the blue of blueprints and of Hokusai's wave, and the pigment that gave cyanide its name rather than the other way round.
Prussian red was an old trade name for a brownish iron-oxide red, and it has nothing to do with Prussian blue except the country.
Puce is French for flea, the name of a dull brown-pink-purple that turned from an insult into the fashionable color of a French court summer.
Pumpkin is the saturated orange of the squash, a name that works as a plain, learnable shade of orange and carries two small stories: Cinderella's coach and a Dutch king's cloak.

Pure Red is the screen value of a paint-industry standard, RAL 3028, but the phrase is older and bigger than any swatch: painters and theorists have argued for centuries about whether a red can be pure at all.
Purple brown is a dark, reddish brown with a violet cast; as a paint name it described the deepest shade of an artificial iron oxide.
Purple madder was a deep, purple-leaning madder lake sold by the English colourman George Field in the early nineteenth century.
Purple Plum is the library's form of Plum Purple, the colour of a ripe plum in one early list of nature's purples.
Purple Red is a descriptive name for a dark red with a violet cast, as ancient as the dye of the murex shellfish and as late as a short-lived nineteenth-century chromate pigment.
Purple Violet is a very dark, reddish plum named in an industrial color standard, and it shows how loosely the words purple and violet are used.
Purple is the color between red and blue that the rainbow leaves out, named after a shellfish dye so costly that for a thousand years it meant the emperor himself.
Purplish grey is a plain description: a grey with a tint of purple, with no history of its own.

Purplish red is a plain description that became a name: a dark wine red entered the mineralogists' color charts in the 1790s and 1820s with a garnet, a garden rose and a bird's quills as its examples.
Putty is the muddy grey-beige of window glazing compound, a color word that was in print by 1889 and that sits, by our count, on about one painting in nine.
Pyrite yellow is a dark, metallic-leaning yellow named for the mineral pyrite, the iron sulfide better known as fool's gold.
Quartz grey is a warm, dark grey with a trace of olive, named in the RAL system for the common mineral.
Queen's blue was one of the named shades of indigo that eighteenth-century English dyers sorted from light to dark, and the books say it was also called royal blue.
Quinacridone magenta is a modern artists' pigment, a deep red-violet that painters use as the magenta primary in color mixing.
Racing green is a very dark green tied in popular memory to British racing cars.
Raspberry red is the red or purplish red of the fruit, a dictionary color word that sits between plain red and crimson.
Raspberry is the red of the berry, a vivid purplish red, and one that naturalists were matching to fruit long before it was an everyday color name.
Raw sienna is the unroasted form of sienna, the Tuscan earth pigment: a yellowish-brown iron-oxide paint that turns reddish only when it is burnt.

Raw umber is the untreated form of umber, a dark brown earth pigment whose color comes from manganese as well as iron; its name most likely means shadow, and painters used it for shadows for about five centuries.
Red Lilac Purple is a pale, faintly pinkish grey-lilac from Patrick Syme's colour nomenclature, number 43 among his purples and illustrated by the pale spots on a peacock butterfly's wing.
Red-orange is the in-between hue of the paint wheel, a name made of two plain color words, and the color most people judge as the warmest.
Red oxide is a generic name for red iron-oxide earths, the red iron-oxide earths, and the books also use it for several other red minerals.
Red-purple is the hue between red and purple on a colour wheel, a name that standards, dictionaries and old pigment books all use, and whose vivid screen version here is nearer to a magenta-red.
Red-violet is the strong, slightly bluish crimson-magenta that sits between red and violet on the color wheel, a name that marks a position more than a thing.
Red wine is a deep crimson-maroon named for the drink, and, as Pastoureau notes, even the drink is not really red but dark.

Red is the color of blood, fire and ripe fruit: often the first hue a language names after light and dark, and for most of Western history the color, so central that one word could mean both red and colored.
Reddish Black is one of the named blacks in the nomenclature that naturalists used to describe moth wings, ducks and ores before color photography.
Reddish brown is a description that became a color name: a dark, strong brown tilted toward red, found in mineral lists, pigment catalogues and painters' grounds long before it was a swatch.
Reddish grey is a grey with a warm red cast, a plain description that old color lists and painting manuals both rely on.
Reddish orange is a descriptive color name from the age of naturalists' charts: number 80 in Patrick Syme's handbook of colors, with a tiger moth's lower wings as its example.
Redwood is a muted brownish red in the ISCC-NBS dictionary; it is also the name of a dyewood family, and the books tie the word to the dye more than to the tree.
Regal is a deep, slightly purple navy, with a name that usually points to purple.
Renaissance is a deep raspberry crimson, a shade name from an early twentieth-century color dictionary; it is not the name of any documented dye or painter's pigment of the period it recalls.
Reseda is a pale green named for the mignonette flower, and the Latin name behind it also belongs to weld, the plant that was Europe's main yellow dye from antiquity to the nineteenth century.
Rhythm is a muted slate purple whose name has no documented origin; the color books mention rhythm only as a quality of color, never as a color.
Rifle green is a dark greyish green, the color of the uniforms of British light infantry rifle regiments.
Roman green is a muted olive. The name belongs to two things: a dull green swatch in the old color atlases, and a 19th-century artists' pigment.
Romanesque is a very dark, slightly reddish purple named in a 1920s color dictionary, a name it shares with the round-arched church style of about 950 to 1150, though no source we hold says why.
Rosa is the Latin word for the rose and the plain word for pink in Spanish, Portuguese and German; as a color name here it is a bright screen pink with no documented maker.
Rose color is a saturated pink-red, and before it was a swatch the phrase described the soft red of madder and safflower preparations.
Rose pink began as a cheap paint: red dye from brazilwood fixed onto chalk, sold to house painters and paper-stainers, and its odd name helped turn the word pink from a method into a color.
Rose-Purple is a light, bright purple-pink from Ridgway's 1886 color book; the books we hold are silent about it, so this is a short article about where the name comes from.
Rose red is the red of a garden rose, a name naturalists fixed on a chart as a pale pink in the early 1800s and one that screens now show as a deep crimson-pink.

Rose is a vivid pink halfway between red and magenta, named after the flower. For most of history, though, the word meant red, and the pink we now call rose had to wait for new dyes and new garden roses to get a name of its own.
Rosewood is a dark brownish red, named for the wood of the rosewood tree.
Rosso corsa is Italian for racing red: the bright red of Italian racing cars.
Rosy Brown is a dusty, pinkish brown, best known today as one of the 140 named colors of the X11 set used on websites.
Rosy Pink is a vivid deep pink from the ISCC-NBS dictionary; the one useful book note is about a different rosy pink, the pale lake made from brazilwood.

Rouge is the French word for red, which English borrowed for the red powders and creams of the face and for the fine red polish of jewellers; the deep, slightly cool red on this page is the shade the word now names.
Royal blue is a deep, vivid blue whose name began as a dyers' grade of indigo and later wandered across smalt, Prussian blue and ultramarine.
Royal purple is a medium-dark blue-violet named for the dye that Roman custom reserved for the emperor, though the name has outlived any single recipe.
Rubber is a plain mid-brown, and the color books say nothing about it as a color: they mention rubber only as a material.
Rubellite is the pink to red variety of tourmaline, a gem name that gives its color to a vivid raspberry-magenta.
Ruber is simply the Latin word for red, a solid basic color term in a language that struggled to name blue and yellow, and the root of the name Rubicon.
Russet is a dark, slightly orange brown, named for a coarse woollen cloth worn by the poor; across the centuries its meaning swung between honest poverty and the color of traitors.
Russian Blue is a pale, greyed blue, a name the books record but barely explain.
Rust brown is a reddish brown named for the corrosion on iron, and the books treat it as a plain descriptive name.
Rust orange is a deep orange named for oxidised iron; a real paint called by this name turns up in a famous American painter's paint box.
Rust is the reddish-brown to orange-red of corroded iron, a color so close to the red earth pigments that chemically they are the same thing.
Saddle Brown is a dark, warm leather brown, one of the 140 named colors in the X11 set for websites.

Saffron yellow is the warm, orange-leaning yellow of the world's costliest spice, the dried threads of one autumn crocus, which dyed Roman gowns, stood in for gold in medieval manuscripts and gave its name to number 68 in Werner's chart of yellows. The threads themselves are crimson; the yellow only comes out in the water.
Sage Green is the soft grey-green of the leaves of the sage plant.
Sage Grey is a greyish olive, listed among the greys and named for the sage plant.
Sage is the soft, greyish green of the leaves of the sage plant; most of the times books say "sage" they mean a wise person, which makes the color's own record unusually thin.
Salmon Color is a soft yellowish pink named after the fish; in the books it appears as the pale untreated look of morganite, a pink beryl.
Salmon pink borrows the flesh of the fish for a warm pink, and the name has been used for a range of colors from rosy pink to orange-red.
Salmon is the orange-pink of the fish's flesh, and on screens it is a bright, warm pink that sits between coral and peach.
Samara is a dark bluish green from Maerz and Paul's color dictionary; our books say nothing about it, and the one book hit is an artist's first name.
Sand Yellow is a warm, muted tan-gold, the color of dry beach sand; for books it is a loose family word, and its sturdiest record is an industrial paint standard.
Sand is the pale, greyish yellow of dry beach and desert ground, a color that painters have long shown as a yellow even though real sand rarely is one.
Sandalwood is a medium reddish brown named for the red dyewood of the red sandalwood tree, whose dye, santalin, gave colormakers browns, purples and a lake pigment.
Sandstone is a muted yellow-tan named for the rock, and the books that define the word do not agree on its shade.
Sandy Brown is a warm light orange-brown, one of the 140 named colors in the X11 web set.
Sandy is a light, warm yellow named for sand; the books say more about the word, which in ochre digging, indigo grading and Pliny's pigment trade mostly meant grain, than about the color.
Sap green is a warm, yellowish, transparent green, named for a paint made from the juice of buckthorn berries and stored in pig bladders, which survives mostly as a name.
Sapphire Blue is a deep, saturated blue named for the gem, and the gem's own name once meant a different stone.
Saratoga is a warm orange-yellow listed in the Maerz and Paul dictionary of 1930; the books say nothing about where the name came from.
Saul is a dark, grey-green name whose origin the books do not record; the only Sauls they discuss are people, among them the Bible's first king of Israel.

Scarab is a strong, slightly bluish green listed in the Maerz and Paul dictionary of 1930; the books do not say where the name came from, but the green-stone scarab of ancient Egypt is a natural association.
Scarlet is a brilliant red leaning toward orange, named after a medieval luxury cloth that could be any color: the red of kermes and cochineal, of cardinals and redcoats, and of the scarlet woman.
Scotch Blue is a very dark purplish blue that entered the early nineteenth-century mineralogist's colour chart as number 24 of the blues, defined by a mixing recipe and three examples from nature.
Sea blue is a medium blue with a green cast, the color of open water as a plain-language name.
Sea green is a medium bluish green with a long life in English: a color of the sea, of emeralds and of dye vats, fixed on screens by the X11 web list as #2E8B57.

Sea is a teal-leaning blue-green, the color we reach for when we paint water; for centuries Europeans drew the sea as green as often as blue, and "sea green" also named a stage in a dye vat, a gem color and half of a pair of opposites.
Seance is a deep violet whose name is a word for a sitting, usually a spirit-medium's.
Seaweed Green is a dark, brownish olive, named for the color of the weed on the shore.
Seaweed is a vivid emerald-leaning green on screen, but the books use the word for something duller: the yellowish green and olive of the real thing.
Sepia is the warm brown ink of the cuttlefish, named with the Greek word for the animal; it dried on drawing papers for centuries and then lent its name to old photographs.
Serpent is a grayish green listed in Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary; nobody records who named it, but green has been the color of serpents in European imagery for centuries.
Shamrock is the bright green of Ireland's clover-like emblem, and the story of how green replaced blue as the Irish color is more tangled than it looks.
Sienna is a brown earth pigment named for the Tuscan city of Siena, and the name now covers a warm reddish brown, deeper and redder than ochre and paler than the umbers.
Signal green is a deep, cool green named for the go-ahead light of traffic signals, and also the name of a fluorescent Day-Glo pigment.
Signal red is a vivid red named for warning lights, and also a trade name for the synthetic pigment para red and for vermilion substitutes.
Silver grey is a cool, slightly bluish mid-grey, named for the metal and an old standard in grey vocabularies.

Silver is the color of the moon's metal, shown on screens as a light neutral grey, though the real thing is all reflection: it paid for empires, drew fine Renaissance sketches in silverpoint, stained medieval glass yellow and underlies photography.
Sinopia is the red earth pigment of the Black Sea port of Sinope; painters later gave its name to the red underdrawing beneath a fresco, and heralds let it drift to green.
Siskin Green is a bright, yellowish olive-green named for a small finch, written into the colour lists of early nineteenth-century naturalists in place of an older name, canary green.

Sky blue is the pale, slightly greenish blue of a clear daytime sky; for most of Western history it was the blue of peasants' woad-dyed clothes, and it became a color of fashion only when indigo made it cheap and bright.
Slate Color is the dark blue-grey of roofing slate, a name that turns up in medicine and paint chemistry as well.
Slate grey is the dark blue-tinted grey of roofing slate, a name that painters, paint makers and fieldworkers have all used loosely.
Slate is the blue-tinted grey of the roofing stone, a color word that books define as dark, mid or bluish and that has spread into a family of twenty-one names.
Smoke is the grey of what rises from a fire: a soft bluish grey in the dictionaries, a darker and warmer one on this swatch, and a word that began in mineral cabinets before it reached the paint box.
Solferino is a bluish crimson-red named after an 1859 battle in northern Italy, first used for the new coal-tar fuchsine dye that was also called magenta.
Somalis is a dusty greyish rose-brown listed in the 1930 Maerz and Paul dictionary; nothing in our books explains the name.
Spanish green is an old name for verdigris, the copper green painters relied on for centuries; the bright green swatch on screens today has little in common with it.

Spanish red is a name with two histories: a bright red earth pigment mined in Spain, and the red of cochineal, the cactus insect whose dye made Spain's American empire rich and sent pirates, spies and chemists after it.
Spectrum Violet is a deep, saturated violet from Ridgway's 1912 atlas; the books do not explain the name, but they do explain why violet is not purple.
Spring Onion is a fresh, moderate yellow-green, the color of the tender shoots, listed in our library from a Japanese traditional color set.
Spruce is a deep, slightly bluish green named for the conifer, though the same word once named a yellow earth pigment and, by one dictionary's count, has also stood for a mauve.
Starling is a dark, warm grey-brown named for the bird; the books say little about it as a color, but our archive shows how common it is in painting.
Steel blue is a mid, slightly greyed blue named for the cold sheen of the metal; on screens it is a CSS color, and in the paint trade it was a term for certain paler grades of Prussian blue.
Steel Grey is a mid, faintly bluish grey named for the metal; it was already a stock term in the mineral colour lists that naturalists borrowed around 1800.
Straw is the pale yellow of dried grain stalks, named for the stalks themselves and listed in chart after chart of color names since the sixteenth century.
Sugar Cane is a pale, warm sand-pink named for the plant; it is a name from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, and the color books we hold say almost nothing about it.
Sulphate Green is a vivid bluish green from Ridgway's 1912 atlas; the books mention sulphates, which gave dyers and pigment makers several green and blue colors, but not this name.
Sulphur yellow is the pale, slightly greenish yellow of the element sulphur, a number in Werner's list of nature's colors that survives today mostly as a shade word.
Sun yellow is a bright, warm yellow-orange named for the sun; it has also been a pigment synonym for a nickel titanium yellow and a dictionary word for maize.
Sunbeam is a soft, dusty gold recorded as a color name in 1917, and the thing it names, a shaft of sunlight in hazy air, is one of the hardest effects in painting.
Sunburn is an old English color word for the brown of sun-tanned skin, listed among the browns of the textile trade.
Sunglow is a bright, golden yellow named for the glow of the sun, and a name found in color charts more than in older books.
Swamp Green is a plain descriptive name for a murky, yellowish olive green; as a listed color it is recent, and the books treat it only as a dictionary entry.
Swedish green is an old trade name for Scheele's green, the copper arsenite pigment invented in Sweden in the 1770s, though one source links the name to a cobalt green instead.
Sweet Pea is a soft pinkish tan named for the flower; the books record the name only in a 1930 color atlas, and say nothing about the swatch's history.
Tan is the color of tanned leather and sun-browned skin, a light yellowish brown whose name comes from the French word that also gave English tawny.
Tangerine is the strong orange of the fruit's skin, a color that is rare as a large area in old paintings but turns up as the spark in many.
Taupe is the French word for a mole, borrowed for a soft brownish grey; in the 1930s two teams of color standardizers found that the shade people called taupe was never quite the color of the animal.
Tawny orange is an old descriptive pairing of two color words, tawny and orange, for a warm brown-orange close to amber.
Tawny is the dull yellowish orange-brown of tan, deer coats and withered grass, a medieval French-derived word that English used for animals, autumn grass and cloth.
Tea Green is a pale, fresh green named in dictionaries for the greyish green of green tea, though the swatch is much lighter than the leaf.
Teal Blue is a moderate greenish blue named for the dark patch on the wings of the teal duck; it is a softer, greyer color than the web-standard teal.
Teal is a dark greenish blue named after the colored band on the wing of a small duck, and on screens it is the web color #008080.
Tennis is a muted olive-gold from the 1930 Maerz and Paul dictionary of color, and it is not the color of a modern tennis ball.
Terracotta is the brownish orange of unglazed fired clay, named from the Italian words for baked earth, and as a tube of paint it was a recipe made to match the pot.
Testaceous is an old descriptive word for the reddish-brown of unglazed tiles and flowerpots, a color most people see every day without the word.
Thistle is a very pale, soft purple, one of the 140 named colors of the X11 set; the books say little about it, and what they say is mostly about the plant.
Tiffany Blue is a trademarked light turquoise tied to one jeweller; the name is a brand's, so the swatch on a screen is only an approximation.

Titanium yellow is a pigment name that books use for more than one thing: a light lemon yellow built from nickel, antimony and titanium oxides, or, in older sources, a yellow made from a titanium ore.
Toga is a dark bluish purple named for the Roman garment, which citizens wore white, magistrates wore edged in purple, mourners wore dark, and only a few men wore purple from edge to edge.
Tomato Red is the orange-red of the ripe fruit; as a web color name it is a modern adoption, and its swatch changes from list to list.
Tomato is the bright orange-red of the ripe fruit, a plant that Europeans grew for two centuries as an ornament before they ate it, and a colour that explains a good deal about how vision works.
Tortoise is the dark mottled brown of tortoiseshell, shown here as one flat reddish brown, which Maerz and Paul recorded as first used in 1730.
True green is the phrase books use for plain, unqualified green, and one book notes that for centuries such a green was hard to dye.
Turquoise green is a pale, cool mint green, and also the trade name of a chromium, aluminium and cobalt oxide pigment that is a good deal bluer than the swatch.
Turquoise is the blue-green of a copper-bearing stone whose French name points at Turkey, and the color has been worked into glaze, glass, smalt and printer's ink ever since.
Tuscan red is a dusky brownish red, and also a pigment name that the old colormen applied to iron-oxide reds sold with a dye lake added.
Tuscany is a dusty pink-brown named for the Italian region, a name whose maker and reason are undocumented, in a region known for its earth, cloth and reds.
Twilight Blue is a descriptive name for the blue of the sky after sunset, which dictionaries describe as greyer than this deep swatch.
Twilight is a muted purplish blue named for the hour after sunset, when the light thins out and the eye begins to trade reds for blues.
Tyrian blue is the blue sibling of Tyrian purple, the shellfish dye, and its best-known story is a religious one.

Tyrian purple was the dye of the ancient Mediterranean, drawn a drop at a time from sea snails at Tyre, and for centuries it meant royalty; the deep wine-red on screen is a modern stand-in for a color that ranged from blue to near black.
Ultra Pink is a hot, electric pink-magenta, most closely tied to the fluorescent crayons of the 1970s and the colors of punk.
Ultra red is an obsolete name for infrared, so the pink swatch here shows only a screen stand-in, not the thing named.
Umber brown is a dark, reddish chestnut brown, number 102 in Patrick Syme's colour chart, named for the earth pigment that painters used for shadows.
Umber is a dark brown earth pigment, rich in manganese, whose name most likely means "shadow"; painters have leaned on it for deep glazes and backgrounds since about the end of the fifteenth century.
Van Dyke Brown is a deep, warm brown named for the painter Anthony van Dyck, though the pigment behind it is a peat-based earth that took his name long after his death.
Vandyke Red is a dark brownish red; as a pigment name it is an old synonym for copper ferrocyanide, a chemical cousin of Prussian blue, and as a swatch it comes from Ridgway's 1912 color atlas.
Veinous Blood Red is a dark, brown-black red from Werner's nomenclature of colors as Syme renamed it, named for the blood of the veins and set beside the brighter red of the arteries.
Velasquez is a deep, wine-colored plum in a 1930 color atlas, spelled without the accent of the Spanish painter it presumably honors.
Velvet is a deep plum-magenta named for the cloth, and the cloth is the better story: for centuries velvet was where Europe's costliest dyes were shown off.
Venet is an old word for a Venice blue, a turquoise-leaning blue that dictionaries link to the Latin for Venetian.

Venetian red is a warm brick-to-orange red iron oxide, named for Venice, that began as a natural earth and by the eighteenth century was largely a factory product made by heating iron sulfate with lime.
Venezia is the Italian name of Venice, used for a deep greenish blue in a 1930 American color dictionary; the books say nothing about it as a color.
Verdigris green is the pale blue-green named for the crust that forms on corroded copper, a pigment that painters from ancient Egypt to the nineteenth century valued and distrusted in equal measure.
Verditter blue is the pale blue-green of a copper pigment that silver refiners stumbled on, an artificial cousin of azurite sold to house painters from the seventeenth century.
Verdure is an old word for the greenness of growing plants, and the swatch is a deep, shaded forest green.
Vermilion Red is the chart color of an early-1800s naturalist's handbook, a brown-tinged scarlet named for the mercury pigment and exemplified by coral, a tomato and the ore cinnabar.

Vermilion is the hot orange-red of mercury sulfide: ground from the ore cinnabar by the Romans, cooked from mercury and sulfur by medieval alchemists, and for a thousand years the red that painters measured every other red against.
Veronese green is a pale yellowish green on modern color charts, but the name belonged to a poisonous copper-arsenic pigment of the 1800s, one the Venetian painter it seems to honor never used.
Very Dark Brown is a plain descriptive name for a brown so deep it is nearly black, and not the name of any dye or pigment.
Vestal is a dusty grey-mauve from a 1930 American color dictionary, and its name points to the Roman priestesses of Vesta, who were dressed in white.
Vibrant Green is a descriptive name for a pure, saturated green; painters long sought strong greens, and verdigris was the best they had until the 1800s.
Viola is a muted violet-purple from a 1930 American color dictionary, named with the Italian word for the violet.

Violet blue is a blue that leans toward purple, a name that Werner's school gave to a mineral color, trade gave to the best grade of cobalt glass, and a modern crayon list gave to the swatch on this page.
Violet Purple is a dark blue-violet from the color list Patrick Syme published in 1814 for naturalists, named by pushing Werner's older violet blue toward purple.
Violet ultramarine, better known as ultramarine violet, is a blue-violet pigment made by chemically altering ultramarine blue.
Violet is the last color the eye can see before light turns invisible: the short-wave end of the rainbow, named after a spring flower, and for most of history a color painters had to fake.
Virgin is a clear mid blue, entered in a 1930 color dictionary under a name that points to the Virgin Mary, whose blue robe is one of the most durable color conventions in Western art.

Viridian is a deep, cool, slightly transparent green made from hydrated chromium oxide, the pigment that replaced a poisonous arsenic green on nineteenth-century palettes and became Cézanne's definitive green.
Viridian is a deep, cool green made from chromium oxide with water in its crystal, first made in Paris about 1838 by a maker who guarded the recipe, and it became Cézanne's definitive green.
Vitreous is the color of glass: in the Maerz and Paul dictionary of 1930 a pale yellow-green, and in most books a word for a mineral's glassy shine rather than for any hue.
Vivid Green is a descriptive name for a saturated green with a blue lean, recorded in Ridgway's color atlas of 1912 and in the ISCC-NBS system of 1955.
Vivid Purple is a fully saturated screen violet that appears in several color lists, and a reminder that paint and dye struggle to reach it.
Warm grey is a grey with a trace of red-brown in it, the color painters call a tinted neutral, and the one the books use mostly as a tool.
Watermelon is the red-pink of the fruit's flesh, a food color name recorded in a 1930 color dictionary and again in the 2010 xkcd survey.
Watteau is a soft sky blue named for the French painter Antoine Watteau (1684-1721), and the pigment he is linked to in the books, Prussian blue, was brand new in his lifetime.
Wedgewood Blue is named for the blue of Wedgwood pottery, but the swatch listed under that name is a pale periwinkle that is much lighter than the famous ware.
Wedgwood blue is a very pale, slightly violet blue whose name comes from ceramics; in our data it is a Ridgway 1912 name.
Wheat is a pale gold, the color of ripe grain in a dry field, and one of the 140 named colors that browsers inherited from the X11 system.
White is the lightest color, the one with no hue at all: the color of chalk, milk and snow, which for most of history was far easier to name than to make.
Windows Blue is the mid blue of Microsoft's Windows desktop, a commercial name that entered color lists only in the 2010s.
Windsor blue is a muted purplish blue; the name is best known as an artists' paint trade name, but the swatch here comes from an older color chart.
Windsor is a deep aubergine-purple in Maerz and Paul's 1930 color dictionary; the books read do not explain the name.
Wine Red is a dark, slightly bluish red named for the drink, and it has been in color charts for centuries, from Maerz and Paul to RAL.
Wisteria is a pale lilac purple named for the climbing vine whose hanging flower clusters fill spring gardens, and in the books it is the color of the gardens more than of any dye.
Wood Violet is a deep blue-purple that appears as a color name in a 1930 dictionary and again as a Pantone name, and that also names a woodland flower.
Xander is a dark olive green that appears in a Wikipedia-sourced color list, and where its name comes from is undocumented in our sources.
Yale Blue is the deep blue of Yale University, which a dictionary of colour calls reddish-blue, and it shares a place on the color charts with a crowd of older blue names.
Yellow grey is a descriptive name for a dull, drab green-yellow-grey, the color of string, and in paintings often a hidden color.
Yellow Stone is a muted greenish yellow-khaki recorded by Maerz and Paul in 1930, which put its first use around 1874.

Yellow is the color of ochre, saffron, lemons and egg yolk, the brightest hue the eye sees and, in poll after poll, the least loved: a color that spent centuries in the shadow of gold and the company of traitors.

Yellowish Brown is a plain two-word name for a warm, mid-toned brown, and one of the descriptive colors that mineralogists wrote into a standard in the 1770s. Its swatch is number 104 in Patrick Syme's color chart, where it was matched to a hoopoe's breast and a guinea pig's spots.
Yellowish green is not a story but a measurement in words: a green with some yellow in it, used for centuries by naturalists, dyers and dictionary makers for everything from lettuce to gemstones.
Yellowish grey is a plain descriptive name that became a numbered standard: entry 13 among the greys in Patrick Syme's 1821 edition of Werner's colour list.
Yellowish orange is a bright saffron yellow-orange, a descriptive name that the books use for dyes and pigments: the carrot, the crocus and a lead-chromate paint.
Zaffre is the name of an impure cobalt oxide that glassmakers and smalt-makers fused with sand and potash; as a color word it names a raw material, and on screens it is a deep, saturated blue.
Zedoary wash is a warm, golden yellow named after a turmeric relative; the name goes back to Robert Dossie in 1764.
Zulu is a very dark brown, listed in Paterson's dictionary as Zulu brown, with no documented origin for the name.
